title: Chemical industry backed laws in three US states to restrict use of air pollution data
text:
As the US’s network for monitoring air pollution deteriorates, a Floodlight investigation has found that the chemical industry is going state-to-state to restrict one of the few options citizens have left for holding polluters accountable: low-cost air sensors.
Over the past two years, the non-profit investigative newsroom determined, lawmakers in Louisiana, Kentucky and Ohio have passed strikingly similar laws barring regulators from acting on air-quality data that communities collect themselves – unless it comes from Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)-approved equipment that typically costs tens of thousands of dollars. Similar legislation has repeatedly been introduced in West Virginia.
In case after case, industry has made the same argument: community monitoring is not reliable enough for regulatory enforcement.
Yet when lawmakers in West Virginia offered a version of a bill that would have let regulators consider community data if it met manufacturer requirements, industry refused to back it.
The bill “essentially codifies what we are trying to prevent”, wrote Jeff Fritz, an official with the chemical giant Chemours, in an internal email. Bill Bissett of the West Virginia Manufacturers Association wrote that the compromise “neuters” the measure and left it “toothless”. That bill died, along with versions in 2025 and 2026.
Ohio slipped its monitor restriction into a budget bill last year, prompting a lawsuit from a group of plaintiffs including Donna Ballinger.
Ballinger has a low-cost monitor in her front yard in Middletown, Ohio, a few hundred feet from a steel plant that she says frequently sends black, white and gray particles on to her property. Fumes sometimes burn her eyes and throat, she said, and she often holds her nose when walking between her house and car.
“My fear is cancer,” she said.
The lawsuit she helped file alleges that the new rules make her monitor’s readings useless as evidence.
An early-warning system in decline
People have turned to low-cost sensors at a time when the public network they used to rely on is thinning out. Federal grants supporting that network have fallen more than 35% over the past two decades, adjusted for inflation, and the number of government air monitors nationwide has fallen by nearly half over the same period, according to EPA data.
Today, nearly six in 10 US counties have no public air monitor at all, according to a 2025 study.
And what remains is showing its age. Leaks, termites and ants plague monitoring stations in one state while officials in another have resorted to shopping on eBay for discontinued parts, according to a 2020 congressional watchdog report. The report doesn’t specify to which states it is referring.
Floodlight examined the largest industrial sources of air pollution in Kentucky, Louisiana, Ohio and West Virginia – and compared the chemicals they reported releasing with what government monitors in those states can detect. At 71 of the 100 facilities examined, the chemical released in the greatest quantity is not measured by any government monitor in the state.
In Louisiana, a national center of oil, gas and petrochemical production, public monitors are often miles from major industrial polluters and fail to test for some of the most dangerous chemicals.
Community groups tried to close that gap. A $500,000 federal grant would have let the Louisiana Environmental Action Network (LEAN) monitor 27 communities it identified as pollution hotspots. But the group installed monitors in only four communities before the Trump administration canceled the grant last year.
“It’s like having your legs knocked out from under you,” LEAN executive director Marylee Orr said.
A multi-state push
Meanwhile, Louisiana lawmakers in 2024 passed the Community Air Monitoring Reliability Act, a law drafted with help from the state’s Chemistry Association that says data used in enforcement must meet EPA-approved standards.
Kentucky followed in 2025, passing a similar measure which requires “scientifically defensible” methods. That phrase had appeared in an American Chemistry Council (ACC) blog post two years earlier. The ACC then lobbied for the Kentucky bill alongside the American Petroleum Institute as well as Chemours and fellow industry powerhouse Dow Chemical.
Kentucky already had proof that monitoring works. Regulators there documented toxic air around Louisville’s industrial Rubbertown, then enacted a plan and revised regulations. As a result, toxic air contaminants across the metro area fell by almost 80%, while the most dangerous chemicals fell by 96%.
The ACC did not answer questions about its lobbying or its role in promoting the state legislation, though it said in a statement that it has invested in community air-monitoring projects and advocated for “expanded access to credible air quality information”.
Chemours spokesperson Jess Loizeaux said the company objects to community-monitoring results being used for enforcement without first verifying their validity and accuracy through official tests by trained regulators.
Ohio’s chemical trade group did not respond to interview requests. But the Ohio Chamber of Commerce’s general counsel, Tony Long, said businesses worry that uncalibrated monitors will spread misinformation. “You don’t want to be stopped for speeding on an uncalibrated speed gun,” he told Floodlight.
In Louisiana, meanwhile, resident Reonda Victor lives in the heavily industrialized corridor between Baton Rouge – the state’s capital – and New Orleans, its most famous city, where air pollution poses one of the highest cancer risks in the US. The closest public monitoring station to her home tests only for lead.
She can’t say whether industrial pollution caused her mother, grandmother and sister to all have breast cancer. But what she knows is she underwent genetic testing, and she showed no predisposition to breast cancer, she said.
And she said she wondered if proper air monitoring could help answer whether industrial pollution factored into her family members’ illness
As she put it: “Without information, we don’t know.”
Read the full investigation at Floodlight

title: An ocean away from Nepal, Sonia spends her spare time piecing together clues about missing flood victims: âI wanted to be usefulâ
text:
A chain of flowers tattooed from knee to foot, a gold nose ring worn on a left nostril, a primary school tie caked in mud: these are the images that linger in Sonia Patil’s mind as she tries to help Nepali flood victims find their loved ones.
More than 1,300 have died and at least 5,500 have been reported missing since a glacial collapse sent a torrent of water, mud, ice and debris through riverside communities along the Nepal-Tibet border on 26 August.
Families and friends of those reported missing have spent weeks searching through graphic photos of bodies, which were uploaded by Nepali police for the community to identify.
Some show only partial corpses – disconnected torsos, limbs splayed at unnatural angles, decomposition eating away at extremities – while in others, the faces of flood victims are turned to the camera, their expressions frozen in their death masks.
Patil, a Melbourne-based chef, has no direct connection with Nepal or any of the people whose loved ones have been reported missing. But when she saw videos of their grief, she knew she could help share their burden.
“It’s a very harrowing task for them,” she says.
“If I had lost a family member, the prospect of coming across their body in that condition would be unbearable.
“I knew I wanted to be useful, it’s the least I can do, even if it’s just being another pair of eyes.”
Almost every day since the disaster, she arrives home at midnight after a 12-hour shift and spends another four to five hours on the Nepali police website, trawling through the hundreds of images of decomposing bodies and limbs.
If any have distinctive features – such as clothes, tattoos and jewellery – she adds them to her list and posts it to Facebook groups filled with those looking for their loved ones.
It can be a confronting and tedious process, Patil says.
During the day, the Nepal police website slows or malfunctions under the weight of all the families looking for information, so she finds it easier to work at night.
The listings, which grow by the day, may only show partial remains, and most only have one image per body – meaning she cannot see any other angles.
Missing persons posters are also spread across multiple platforms, forcing Patil to search across the internet to crosscheck information.
But no matter how hard it is, she says it is worse for those on the ground.
“It’s very disturbing to know that I may be looking at a picture of a live person and somebody who is deceased at the same time, trying to compare them,” she says.
“I find it easier when I go in with the mindset that all the images on that website are all human: they have lived lives, they have stories, they have families looking for them.”
Patil is part of a group which includes people from the US, Europe, New Zealand and other countries who work together to identify bodies. They generally look for matches for those who have reached out to them with photos of their missing friends and family.
It is difficult to be 100% certain through visual identification alone, as many images of the bodies are unrecognisable. So when members think they have made a match, the group asks relatives to submit their DNA to labs in Nepal for official confirmation.
If they believe they have made a match for someone who has not asked for their help, the group tries to report it to Nepali authorities.
Making a likely identification is bittersweet for everyone involved, Patil says, because while they are glad a family will get closure, “it’s not a great feeling to know that person is no longer here”.
But it is worse when she posts her lists and no one responds.
“In some cases, entire families have been wiped out, which means that even people with the most recognisable tattoos have nobody left to identify them,” she says.
Patil does not want any thanks for her work. Instead, she urges everyone to keep sharing the lists in case someone in their network recognises the missing.
It is now becoming harder to discern any distinctive features as the bodies disintegrate under the sun and sludge with the passing days. But Patil has vowed to continue.
“So long as I can find tattoos or anything identifiable, I will keep going,” she says.

title: Nepal says big polluters must âwake upâ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
text:
Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.
Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.
Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.
Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.
In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.
“This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”
Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.
“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”
For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.
“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”
Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.
Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.
While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”
He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.
The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.
Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.
“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.
He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.
Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.
“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.
“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

title: What we know about the link between Nepalâs flash floods and our climate crisis
text:
At 8.37am local time last Wednesday, a huge mass of rock and ice sheared free from a mountain, sliding 1,200 metres to the valley floor in Nepal’s Langtang national park, about 60km north of the country’s capital, Kathmandu.
Horrifying images and videos soon emerged of a torrent of mud, water and debris that swept down the Lhende Khola valley at speeds approaching 150km/h. Flowing down the Lhende Khola, Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers that run between Tibet and Nepal, the flood water swept away homes, roads, bridges and power plants. Along the Trishuli, water levels rose by as much as nine metres in half an hour. As of the time of writing, the death toll of the disaster approached 1,000 people, with more than 4,400 on both sides of the border missing.
As the rescue effort continued – hampered by bad weather, poor access and the threat of further flooding due to two lakes that have formed after the landslide – Nepali prime minister Balendra Shah said the catastrophe was “not an ordinary” event.
Shah said on social media that “the risks we face in the Himalayan region are increasing alongside climate change … It is now time for us to strongly raise with the international community the issue of the disasters we are experiencing as a result of climate change.”
More on the scale of this disaster and what it tells us about our climate crisis, after this week’s headlines.
In focus
What caused last week’s catastrophe was not immediately clear: initial reports suggested the floods could have been caused by an earthquake in the area that triggered a landslide, while early satellite imagery suggested that a glacial collapse was to blame. Subsequent satellite analysis showed that bedrock underneath a glacier collapsed, with the landslide registering as a magnitude 5.2 seismic event.
“It seems that a massive rock face with the glacier on top of it has essentially gone,” says Adrian McCallum, a senior lecturer in geotechnical engineering at the University of the Sunshine Coast in Australia. One seismologist called the landslide “one of the largest in the last decade or two in the world”.
As Nepal’s Shah said in his statement, our environmental crisis cannot be separated from this disaster. The Himalayas – spanning Nepal, India, China, Bhutan and Pakistan – are warming twice as fast as the global average, putting the region at increased risk of avalanches, landslides and floods. The UN said in 2023 that Nepal’s mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.
While scientists haven’t definitively linked the Lhende Khola landslide to the climate crisis, they have pointed out that rising temperatures mean permanently frozen mountain slopes are at risk of melting and destabilising.
“Increased temperatures result in increased melt, which results in increased water,” McCallum says. “Movement of water into voids within either soil or rock … destabilises what once may have been a more solid rock mass or soil environment.”
With global heating, mountainous areas are also at risk of permafrost degradation, “glacial lake outburst floods” (GLOFs), and increasingly erratic rainfall, raising flood and landslide risk.
Glacial lakes form behind natural dams as a result of glacier melt, and can cause catastrophic outburst floods if their natural dam walls are breached. More than 12,000 deaths have been attributed to such floods globally.
Given the risks to downstream communities in the Himalayas, scientists have pointed to the need for early warning systems, which would require coordinated international monitoring efforts.
“Wherever the glaciers are receding … you have the potential for a GLOF to occur,” McCallum says, such as in the European Alps and the South American Andes. In North America, an outburst flood causes periodic problems in Juneau, the capital of Alaska.
To be clear, there was no GLOF involved in last week’s landslide. But Nepal has more than 2,000 glacial lakes, and 21 of those, according to the UN, are considered potentially dangerous.
As climate academic Bill McGuire wrote for the Guardian this week, global heating will “leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.”

title: Minister tells Brits to stock up on days of supplies after âsupersizeâ El NiÃ±o warning
text:
British people have been urged to have enough food and water on hand to survive a few days without power or water, as the UN said the El Niño climate phenomenon was “supersizing before our eyes”, exacerbating extreme weather events worldwide.
Forecasters say they are braced for the biggest El Niño in 1,000 years, bringing wildfires and floods to parts of the world, and the threat of a wet, stormy winter for the UK.
 As the British government plans a campaign urging citizens to prepare for national emergencies, Angela Eagle told the Guardian the likelihood of a wild winter showed the importance of keeping supplies at home.
The environment secretary said: “We’re about to experience probably the largest El Niño that has ever been seen, and that will lead to drier summers, wetter winters, with more extreme storms in this country.
 “It will do a lot more damage in Asia with flooding, and therefore I think that we need to take it seriously.
 “If you’ve got a store of a bit of food that can keep you going for a while before the emergency services can get to you, you’re going to be a lot better off than if you haven’t. So some of it is that kind of preparation for just being a bit more resilient.”
El Niño is a natural climate cycle where wind changes over the Pacific lead to rising ocean temperatures and the transfer of huge amounts of heat to the atmosphere.
The most recent data, from Monday, shows the temperature of the ocean at the heart of El Niño at 2.6C above the 30-year average. That is already close to the highest anomaly ever recorded in the satellite data era, 3.1C in 2015, with months to go before the peak is expected.
That peak is forecast to reach about 4C in November, according to the average of 14 different models. Zeke Hausfather, a climate analyst, said data from analysis of corals, tree rings and historical documents suggested no El Niño had reached this level in the last millennium. Any temperature anomaly above 0.5C is classed as an El Niño.
The El Niño is likely to be the largest in at least 1,000 years and will pile extra heat into an atmosphere where temperatures are already rising rapidly due to global heating. The combination means 2027 is set to “blow apart” the record and be the hottest year ever recorded.
António Guterres, the UN secretary general, said: “El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up.
“The world is in the danger zone of extreme weather. The race now is between rising risks and our commitment to take climate action and protect people. We must win that race.”
Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the UN’s World Meteorological Organization (WMO), said: “El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world. We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies.”
The climate crisis, caused by pollution from fossil fuels, is already supercharging extreme weather and killing people, with the most extreme heatwave ever recorded hitting Europe this summer and leading to at least 35,000 deaths.
The El Niño will ratchet up the effects even further, with the scale of the event having been described as “truly mind-blowing” and a “Godzilla-level” event.
  The rising heat from the El Niño is already having effects, from worsening wildfires in Indonesia to the weakening of vital monsoon rains in India. The effects will spread globally, from greater fire risk in Australia to more intense floods in South America. The World Food Programme said in August that the El Niño was likely to push about 50 million people into acute hunger.
In the UK, ministers are prioritising climate resilience after the UK’s hottest summer on record.
A campaign from the Cabinet Office in the coming months will tell households to stock up on tinned food and take steps to ensure they are prepared for national emergencies.
Meanwhile Eagle will oversee farming improvements and a new programme of reservoir building that she says will leave Britain better prepared than it has been for the kind of extreme weather that is likely in future years.
Speaking from Havant Thicket, which is set to be the country’s first new reservoir since 1992, Eagle said the country had not been good enough at preparing for climate-related emergencies in the past and would have to change its farming and water management techniques.
 “We need to do our own adaptations … and that is what things like these this reservoir is about,” she said.
“It’s what the farming transition is about, so we can farm in a more resilient and and sustainable way from an environmental point of view.”

title: Climate injustices have been laid bare in the Nepal-Tibet flood disaster
text:
The recent glacial collapse and catastrophic floods in Nepal and Tibet are not isolated tragedies (Report, 28 August). They reflect accelerating climate disruption that disproportionately affects the countries and people that are least responsible for global emissions.
As climate change intensifies, glaciers around the world, including in the Himalayas, are melting at unprecedented rates, destabilising ecosystems and causing glacial collapse and ice-and-rock landslides, destroying settlements, villages and livelihoods in minutes. No one died when a Swiss glacier collapsed last year, owing to early-warning systems that were in place. But a lack of early-warning systems means that the disaster in Nepal and Tibet has led to hundreds of deaths and thousands missing.
Events like these are not “natural disasters”. They are due to global warming and climate injustices, and also flawed development policies, including rampant property developments on vulnerable floodplains. They call for better disaster preparedness and investment in early-warning systems. Most importantly, they require global action.
The UK has long positioned itself as a leader in international development and climate action. Yet recent UK commitments have fallen far short of what is required – including the decision to raid the diminished aid budget to switch international climate finance grants to loans, to fund a bus-fare cap.
The foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, recently spoke compellingly about the need to put the climate crisis and overseas development at the heart of UK international relations. These words must now translate into action. The UK must step up its development commitments and funding for climate adaptation, and loss and damage, to support those living on the frontlines of climate change.
The recent glacial floods remind us that climate disruption is global, and highly unequal. The UK must act urgently. Anything less is a failure of responsibility.
Prof Lyla Mehta
Institute of Development Studies
Sunil Acharya is correct when he states: “The countries that benefited most from fossil fuel-driven growth have a responsibility to cut emissions rapidly” (Nepal-Tibet flood: this is the cost of not acting in the face of the climate crisis, 28 August).
This was the founding principle of the global “contraction and convergence” framework, tabled by India, China and the African Group of Nations in Kyoto at Cop3 in 1997.
Had we enacted this, we would now be on a safe, and equitable, 30-year contraction path, avoiding the worst of the climate crisis and ensuring our survival. Instead, we remain adrift, with no viable solution or plan. Is it really too late to adopt this framework?
Lynda McDonald
Portaferry, County Down
 The key question is: who should pay for this disaster? Yes, the rich world should pay, but the bills should be sent to all the fossil-fuel companies that have known this risk for at least half a century and have ignored it. If they refuse to pay, all of us in countries that have profited from the fossil-driven benefits of “progress” should, through our governments, pay a progressive tax on all things based on fossil fuels, to cover the past, present and future costs of climate change. 
Jan Bengtsson
Uppsala, Sweden

title: After the flood: human suffering on an unfathomable scale in Nepalâs worst-hit districts
text:
Searching for the body of his wife in the mud, Dil Bahadur Shrestha lamented that he did not even have a shovel left. For now, he has been using his hands to try to find her as he picks through the ruins of his house.
On Wednesday morning last week, Jamuna Shrestha, his wife of 50 years, had been at home in Betrawati on the banks of Nepal’s Trishuli River, feeding her beloved chickens and goats.
As deadly flash floods coursed down the river valley, Jamuna was last seen going back into her house, trying to usher her chickens to safety, while others fled uphill. Now that house stands like a muddy carcass, everything inside it destroyed or washed away by the violent force of the water and debris that killed more than 1,200 people in Nepal and Tibet.
Dil Bahadur Shrestha, 70, had been tending to his rice fields and feeding his cows on the opposite bank when he felt the ground tremble and saw a black wave, hundreds of metres high, coming down the valley. He ran to safety in the forest, but not before watching two bridges get swept away behind him. “When it hit, everything was destroyed within two minutes,” he said.
He knows in his heart that his wife is gone, but like thousands caught up in the disaster, her body has yet to be found and she is counted among the missing. More than 5,000 people are reported missing in Nepal and a further 546 in the Tibet region of China.
Rescue workers have still not reached Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s home, so he returned to try to retrieve her body himself. “Maybe she thought the flood wouldn’t reach inside the house,” he said, wiping away tears.
The couple had already rebuilt their home once after an earthquake in 2015 that killed about 9,000 people. As he spoke, his frail body collapsed to the barren, muddy ground where his neighbour’s house once stood.
“Even now, I cannot believe that she is gone,” he said. “I cannot forget her. That’s why I keep walking around looking for her. I still feel as if she might be walking around somewhere here. I keep getting this feeling that she might still be here, looking after the chickens and the goats.”
The scale of the tragedy in Betrawati is unfathomable. It was 8.37am when a melting glacier high up in the Himalayas on the border between Nepal and Tibet crashed into the valley below, setting off deadly flash floods down Nepal’s Bhotekoshi and Trishuli rivers. By 8.50am, with only a few minutes’ warning, the settlement of Betrawati was engulfed.
This once-thriving market town was submerged in mud so thick that only the top two floors of a six-storey building are visible. Most houses were washed away entirely or flipped on their sides by the sheer force of the floods. School buses lie overturned. A grocery shop was swept 200 metres from its original location and lies in ruins. The river itself has diverted to a new path that cuts through where the highway once was.
Fragments of the lives of the thousands who lived here lie scattered in the debris: kettles, teddy bears, a record-keeping book, saucepans, medicine packets, a pair of glasses. At least 250 people are missing, Dil Bahadur Shrestha’s brother and sister-in-law among them.
As Dil Bahadur Shrestha surveyed the ruins of his life, search and rescue teams stood on the opposite bank, looking for the dead. By the end of the day, they had pulled 24 bodies from a single house. A helicopter thundered overhead, white body bags swinging underneath.
“I feel there could still be hundreds of bodies here,” said Dil Bahadur Shrestha. “So many people were swept away all at once, carried off by the raging water.” His voice broke: “Now I’m alone. I am completely alone.”
A few metres away, Santamaya Lawat, 57, stood shaking a thick cake of dirt from the few clothes and blankets she had been able to retrieve from her brother’s home, now only partly standing, with a gaping hole in the side. Her own house, built just 10 months ago with her life’s savings, was still so filled with mud she had not yet been able to get inside. Five members of her family are gone.
“My heart broke when I came back,” she said. “This was supposed to be the house I lived in for the rest of my life, but everything is gone. It was like heaven here and now it has been turned into hell.”
Further up the river, in the district of Rasuwa, on the border with Tibet, the scale of destruction only gets worse. Many of the villages here were swept away entirely and are only accessibly by army helicopter. Some are still so cut-off and the ground conditions so precarious that the fate of hundreds of people remains unknown. On Tuesday, police search and rescue teams confirmed they had finally been able to begin ground operations in the border village of Timure, recovering 90 bodies so far.
A week after the disaster, survivors who fled up mountainsides were still being collected by army helicopters and evacuated to the army base in Dhunche, Rasuwa district’s administrative headquarters.
The mountain village of Syabru Besi was among those wiped clean away, with even the road to the village gone. According to local government officials, at least 500 people there are missing, a quarter of the population. The village resembles nothing more than a muddy riverbed, just one building left standing.
Chhiring Dorje, a 50-year-old farmer, was among those who managed to escape Syabru Besi, but five of his family are missing. “There were 15 or 16 of us from the village who made it safely to the forest,” said Dorje. “We stayed there for two days before the army came in a helicopter. We had nothing to eat. We survived by drinking water from the forest.”
He stood tightly holding the hand of his nine-year-old granddaughter, Ritu Tamang, who wore a big pink rucksack as they waited at Dhunche army base for a ride down to Kathmandu. Rescue helicopters thundered in and out every few minutes. She said quietly that there was “nothing left where our house used to be. I used to go to school and was in Grade 1. Now the school is gone. There are no teachers either.”
With the highways washed away, the only road from Kathmandu to Rasuwa is a perilous unpaved track of mud and stones, weaving through tiny mountain villages. The journey often takes more than 12 hours. The treacherous conditions have made it difficult for aid to reach the worst-hit areas and hindered the rescue and relief operations. Many aid trucks are now stuck in Dhunche, unable to drive further north.
At a small relief camp on the road between Betrawati and Dhunche set up by Nepal’s Dhulikhel hospital, people collected medicine and food supplies. Doctors said dozens of the children here had lost their parents in the floods. More than 200 children from the local Nilakantha school, most aged between five and 11, are also missing, believed to have been washed away as they walked to morning classes.
Prakash Nepal, a teacher, said the school had received a warning just 10 minutes before the flood waters hit, when the school bus was already picking up students.
“Luckily, we immediately contacted the bus driver and the vehicle stopped midway so the students were able to survive,” he said. “The surge of water did reach the vehicle, but thankfully it did not cause much damage.”
However, many of the local families had been displaced by the 2015 earthquake and still lived in informal settlements along the riverbank. Most of those children had been walking to school when the flood struck. Prakash Nepal’s eyes welled with tears: “We could not save the students who were still on the road.”
Amid the tragedy, there were also small stories of hope. Sitting on the porch of their village home in Lachyang, Ram Krishna Neupane, 69, and his wife, Muiya Neupane, 66, said their only son had been working as a vet in Syabru Besi when the village was hit.
For two days afterwards they heard nothing and feared he was dead. Then they received a phone call. “He called up from a hospital in Kathmandu; he had been rescued by the army,” said Ram Krishna Neupane. “He could not speak, he was crying so much and we were crying.”
It was, added his wife, “a miracle”.

title: As Nepalâs morgues fill, Parkrit hopes her DNA can be used to find her mother
text:
An army official calls out a name. A young woman stands, two pieces of identification in her hands. She fills out a form, takes another and moves to the back of the hospital to give a vial of blood.
With so many people killed by Nepal’s floods, and hundreds of bodies being buried because the morgues are full, there is now a push to identify victims through DNA. The woman, Prakrit Gurung, 19, is hoping her DNA will be linked to her mother’s body. Her father’s has been found – her brother recognised his picture on a wall outside the hospital.
At the government’s request, Gurung is one of dozens lining up on Tuesday morning. Earlier, an Australian citizen was one of the first 14 people to attend. He had flown over to be with his family – his brother, a Nepali citizen, is missing.
Authorities are asking relatives abroad to have their DNA profiles sent over. Several Australian families have already had samples taken.
“We are collecting the blood samples here, from their siblings, or direct relatives,” says Rameshwor Adhikari from the army. “People are coming from all over the valley to give blood, and from different places all over the country.”
Adhikari adds: “It is a disaster. A natural calamity.”
The first day they set up 37 people came through but numbers are growing – and the army brings out more shade tents for people to sit under.
Adhikari wants as many people as possible to come forward. There are now more than 1,000 people confirmed dead and nearly 4,000 reported missing. As of Wednesday morning, 38 of them are Australians.
In a statement this week, family members of 25 missing Australians called for more government support to “bring our friends and loved ones back home”.
Nepali families from the worst-hit area, the upper Rasuwa district, have been campaigning for their government to do more to get boots and rescue equipment on the ground.
It has been a week since the floods and contact has still not been established in some places along the Chinese border.
Lhakpa Gha’s village, Timure, is one of them. Standing outside a Buddhist monastery on Tuesday afternoon, the 53-year-old says that if she talks, the tears will come.
And as she lists her relatives who were washed away, they do. Her father, brother-in-law, son, daughter-in-law, their four-year-old daughter, her daughter and her sister’s brother. All seven, gone.
Gha and her husband survived because they were in Kathmandu, looking after two of their grandchildren attending school here.
“I lost my whole family,” she says through a translator. “We’ve lost everyone.”
The monastery is housing about 200 people from the upper region who managed to survive – they were higher up on the mountain when the flood hit. Many watched as their loved ones were swept away, their towns flattened.
“The army has not been able to reach the village,” Gha says. “They keep saying our village is high risk but we don’t understand. We are fighting with them. If it’s high risk, you need to act. But they have just said they can’t get in.”
Her son and daughter were doctors in the village – they stayed in Timure so they could keep providing for the family.
“We have nothing,” Gha says. “We depended on my son for money.”
On Monday a UN report into the conditions in the country’s far north said it could take weeks to reach the upper areas – there are hardly any roads left in, and bridges have been washed away.
If the army cannot get in, nor can the aid groups. Amy Sagitta Lefevre from Save the Children says: “Aid is definitely getting through, but to a point.”
Speaking from the agency’s warehouse in Kathmandu, she says its teams have reached Rusawa by road. Aid they can’t get further is stored at the army barracks.
“The challenging bit for rescue workers is the same challenging bit for aid organisations, because we have the same access issues as they do,” she says.
Save the Children is getting kits up the valley that include makeshift tents, so people have somewhere to shelter. It’s also setting up mobile toilets.
“On the ground we’re giving out non-food items,” Lefevre says, “which are blankets, ropes, tarpaulin sheets – because a lot of people are sleeping exposed to the elements, so just sheets in case they need to be protected from the rain.”
Many of the shelters up the valley are overcrowded, so families are being sent farther afield.
“We’re also giving out things like buckets, just so people can carry things or wash, if need be.
“And then we have what we call dignity kits … they’re aimed at women, but specifically pregnant women – they have an extra sari, some of the mothers need clothes because they’re still wearing the same clothes they were wearing the day of the disaster.”
About 2,600 children are expected to need medical treatment for “severe wasting” and more than 100 may have been separated from their parents.
Lefevre says it’s impossible to put a timeline on anything. But recognising that the full recovery process could take over a year, Save the Children has set up a field office.
Its workers are worried about the spread of disease, water contamination, overcrowded shelters and the potential, in the chaos of the recovery, for children to be trafficked.
“This area of Nepal has historically been a hotbed for child trafficking of girls,” she says. “We’ve heard anecdotally that it may have lessened in recent years, but because of this disaster we are now very concerned about the fact that children or girls … could be trafficked.”

title: Nepal-Tibet flood deaths pass 1,000 as police ask relatives for DNA to identify victims
text:
Nepali rescuers have built temporary bridges to reach remote areas and dug through the ruins of hydropower projects in the Himalayas to rescue hundreds of trapped workers, as the death toll passed 1,000 nearly a week after devastating floods left a trail of destruction across the country’s towns and valleys.
About 600 people remain stuck in several devastated hydropower stations that have become the focus of rescue efforts. The prime minister, Balendra Shah, said more than 11,000 people had been rescued across the affected region, and power and communication lines had been restored in some areas.
“Thousands of citizens have lost their homes, families, loved ones and property,” Shah said.
Six days after the catastrophe struck the Himalayan border region, 4,400 people were still missing in Nepal and Tibet. Police in Kathmandu have urged relatives of missing tourists to provide DNA samples to assist identification efforts.
In a statement posted to social media, Nepal police on Monday asked relatives of those missing to “provide a fresh blood sample for DNA profiling and two passport-sized photographs” to the pathology laboratory at the Nepal police hospital in Kathmandu, or the nearest district police office.
Among Nepal’s list of the missing are 592 foreigners, including tourists who had come for mountain trekking and Hindu pilgrims seeking spiritual peace at Tibet’s sacred Mount Kailash, from countries such as India, the US, UK, Australia and Canada.
Relatives abroad have been requested to undergo DNA profiling at an authorised laboratory and to “send a soft copy of the DNA profile to Nepal police’s official email address”.
In some of Nepal’s flood-affected areas, hundreds of unidentified bodies have already been buried because they are decomposing and there is no room left in hospitals or morgues.
At the police hospital in Kathmandu on Tuesday, more than 100 people were waiting to have their blood sampled.
Among them was Prakaiti Jurnj. Her mother was still missing, but the family had been able to identify her father’s body from a photograph on the wall outside the teaching hospital, where images of the deceased have been posted in an effort to identify the victims.
“Both my father and mother, they were in the village in Nukawot. They were both swept away by the flood,” she said. “We haven’t heard from them since Wednesday. We found my father’s body; my brother saw the photo on the wall.”
She was waiting for her two other siblings, who live in the UK, to arrive on Tuesday so they could all try to get up to the village. She said she wanted to contact her grandmother or sister-in-law, who she thinks both survived the flood because their house is further up the mountain. Their village was still in a blackout, and making contact was impossible.
“I can’t go there; the situation is very bad,” she said. “I can’t go up there alone. I am not sure if we’ll be able to get them.”
The disaster was triggered by a glacier collapse that sent a deluge of ice, rock and mud through Nepal’s border region with China, posing a massive challenge for the country’s six-month-old government.
The region is vulnerable to flooding and landslides, and extreme weather events such as intense monsoons and melting glaciers have become more common because of warming due to human-caused climate change.
In a late-night social media post, Shah said aid worth more than $42m had poured into the country, but that Nepalis were reeling. “The government understands the immense pain they are enduring. The path ahead is to support them through this suffering and help them return to normal life through rehabilitation,” the prime minister said.
Shah also said that 279 workers had so far been rescued from hydropower projects, where authorities estimated close to 1,000 people had been trapped. Days after the disaster, hope was rapidly diminishing that any of those trapped in a series of tunnels could be alive.
Pictures and videos shared by rescue teams showed earth-moving equipment digging and shovelling mud and rocks under lights in the dark of the night. Soldiers used torchlight in a big pit they had created to look for space to get into one tunnel.
Chinese state media coverage has focused largely on the official response, highlighting the deployment of firefighters, the People’s Liberation Army and instructions from top leaders. Little is known about victims on the Chinese side.
The flood was “caused by glacier instability under the long-term effects of global warming”, China’s state broadcaster said on Monday.
Shah said the catastrophic event signalled the growing risks that the Himalayan region faces. “The region must therefore remain vigilant. The time has come for us to strongly raise before the international community the disasters we are experiencing as a consequence of climate change,” he wrote in his post.

title: US border patrol expected to aid Grand Canyon search for missing person
text:
A US border patrol technical search team is expected to deploy in the Grand Canyon, as authorities continue the search for at least one missing person after a fatal flash flood washed through the national park over the weekend.
Authorities are rushing to scour the area as more heavy rain and thunderstorms in weather forecasts threaten additional debris flows, flash floods or rock falls.
Nearly 80 people have been rescued since a torrent of water swept through the national park on Saturday, and two people have been confirmed dead. They were identified by their families as chiropractor John Giusti, 46, and martial arts studio owner Brent Rosenkranz, 42, who had been hiking together.
A third friend who had joined the trip, 53-year-old pilot Timothy Smith, was still missing. The men had been camping at the bottom of the Grand Canyon since Friday.
Searchers used night vision and other equipment to find people who needed rescuing during the deluge, incident commander Dave Black said during a Monday evening press conference.
Rangers referred to the park’s permit system and checked vehicle license plates to track the number of missing people. “As of right now, they have no reason to believe, from the tips we’ve been through so far, that there’s anybody besides the one” missing person, Black said.
The flood happened deep in the canyon on Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the Colorado River near Phantom Ranch. The fabled lodge has been a beacon for half-collapsed, exhausted and overheated hikers for more than a century.
Hiker Daniel Evans said it had rained several times before the worst 30-minute downpour Saturday afternoon. He had been planning to rest through the hot day and spend the night near the hard-hit Bright Angel campground area.
Earlier, rangers told him it looked to be safe. Then, as the rain poured, they told him it was time to go.
Flash floods are not uncommon in the Grand Canyon. In summer, during the monsoon season, clear days can quickly give way to thunderstorms and heavy downpours. The region’s dry landscape can absorb only a limited amount of water. What might be a normal summer downpour somewhere else can become a charging wall of water in a rocky canyon.
But this weekend’s flood was probably intensified by a confluence of climate factors, including drought, wildfire scarring and warming temperatures in the Pacific Ocean that can supercharge storms.
This year’s monsoon is especially intense because there is a higher amount of water vapor in the atmosphere, mostly because of a strong El Niño, said A Park Williams, a hydroclimatologist at the University of California, Los Angeles. El Niño is part of a natural cycle, but models show there is a strong likelihood this will become one of the strongest on record.
El Niño layers on top of spikes in temperature fueled by the climate crisis. Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis will create stronger extremes and destructive shifts between wet and dry conditions. As temperatures continue to climb, extreme events will not just increase – they will become more likely to overlap.
Saturday’s strong storm also hit part of the burn scar of the Dragon Bravo wildfire, a destructive and fast-moving blaze that swept across nearly 150,000 acres (60,700 hectares) and consumed the historic Grand Canyon Lodge in July 2025.
Runoff tends to flow more quickly in the aftermath of a fire, especially in hotter burns where slopes are left bare of vegetation.
The flood also damaged the water pipeline that serves visitors and the roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.
Early assessments showed roughly 40% of the pipeline had been damaged or destroyed.

title: âThe mountains are changingâ: What the floods tell us about the future of Indiaâs Himalayas
text:
It has been hard not to despair while watching the ruinous floods swallow parts of Nepal, and harder, still knowing that the agony compounds each passing day for dozens of Indian families whose members remain unaccounted for.
Social media is awash with desperate pleas, photos and details of the young and old, men and women, from Mumbai to Kolkata, posted by families searching for traces of life. The disaster unfolded when a melting glacier slammed into the valley below, unleashing a deadly cascade of rock and ice down the Bhote Kashi River, which flows from Tibet into Nepal.
Among the 275 Indians missing at the time of writing are workers of a hydropower project and people undertaking the Hindu pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet. Another 128 people of Indian origin, including a large group of Sadhguru’s Isha Foundation spiritual group, are also missing; 149 Indian people have been rescued as of Monday.
For Gauri Joshi, whose five relatives remained unaccounted for over the weekend, the last few days have been a blur of calling their numbers in vain, watching news of rescue operations and trying to reach Indian officials – over and over again. What she has pieced together so far is that her relatives, part of a pilgrim tour group from Maharashtra, cleared immigration at the Gyirong border between Nepal and Tibet and boarded buses shortly before the flood waters destroyed the crossing.
“Chances appear very bleak now. But maybe a miracle will happen,” Joshi said.
The tragedy has reignited the question of how vulnerable the Himalayas are to climate change, and what its implications are for India. To understand the risks of glacier collapse and thawing permafrost leading to sudden floods and debris flows, I spoke to Dr Ashim Sattar, a professor at Indian Institute of Technology Bhubaneswar and an expert on glacial lake outburst floods. The conversation has been edited and condensed.
What are the climate- or glacier-related risks emerging across the Himalayas?
“There are different forms of cryosphere and how they pose a hazard. In a layperson’s terms, the cryosphere is where water exists in solid form, for example a glacier. When it melts, it forms glacial lakes. If they have an outburst, they can cause damage downstream.
Another cryospheric component is glacier ice. This is what we’ve seen in Nepal, where a glacier detachment happened. The frontal part of the glacier detached from the main glacier and eventually led to a debris flow.
The third component is permafrost. They exist widely in the Himalayas, but there has not been much monitoring because it’s very difficult. Everything – these lakes, glaciers and permafrost – are all hazards. Unless they’re triggered, they would not cause damage.
With climate change, these grounds will go above zero degrees and will start to degrade. These would need very little … to mobilise debris. We might expect a higher frequency of debris flows in the future. We won’t know how they are getting conditioned, unless we have some monitoring stations and scientific investigation.
And given the Himalayas are very vast, monitoring every part of it becomes tricky. It can be the mountain ranges within India, or maybe outside India, eventually, which drains into the Indian subcontinent. That needs to be well studied.”
How big are the downstream risks for India?
“Right now, this is a gap in scientific studies; nothing [is] quantified yet. There is direct evidence of climate impacts, even in the Indian part of the Himalayas. The number of glacial lakes is increasing, the size of glacial lakes is increasing, the volume of glacial lakes is increasing, and glaciers are retreating. The risk exists because it might happen any time.”
Which parts of India are the most vulnerable?
“Everyone in the Himalayas, every Himalayan state has hazards. We can’t deny it. If you look at the eastern side, they have a lot of glacial lakes. They have already reached their maximum extent. Most full-grown lakes are about to reach their limits, like maximum extent. In the western Himalayas or even the central Himalayas, there’s a lot of scope for the lakes because they have not reached their full extent. As the glaciers would retreat, they would keep on growing.
We are still unsure when the status is going to change for any of these states. That’s a very, very difficult question, and I don’t think anyone [can] answer it at this moment without any scientific investigation.”
How would you describe India’s early warning systems and disaster preparedness?
“The National Disaster Management Authority is taking proactive steps now with the glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF) Risk Mitigation Programme to install early-warning systems.
Maybe an early warning system should be community-based. It should be for the people and by the people. It’s not always the scientist or the policymakers who can actually make this work at its full potential. We need to have local knowledge, involve the communities to make them more effective.”
How long will it take to have these systems in place?
“I have no idea because each of these organisations are working at their own pace. They have their own style of working. I’m sure it is going to happen soon. I can just comment on the areas where I know, and I’ve been in touch.”
Is prevention possible, or can it only minimise the damage?
“Prevention is possible, but it is very expensive: computationally, financially and manpower-wise. Minimising is also possible. It would require a lot of intervention in the high mountains, which is very difficult in those terrains.
We know that the mountains are changing and the hazard levels are increasing, so the only way forward is to minimise the exposure to the risk below. That means how much of the hazard is going to interact with the downstream. If something is in the path, we remove them.”
To support relief efforts in Nepal, you can contribute to the prime minister’s Disaster Relief Fund here.
What else we’re reading about
RSS in New York | Last weekend, Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) chief Mohan Bhagwat addressed Indian Americans at New York’s Madison Square Garden calling for global unity. The Quint reported that the newly formed group behind the event has RSS links. The visit was opposed by several diaspora groups that reject the RSS’ Hindu nationalist ideology and criticise its record on minority rights.
Books and backlash | A reading session organised in Ahmedabad after a private school was forced to drop books by Malala Yousafzai and Anne Frank was allegedly disrupted by a group affiliated with the rightwing Bajrang Dal. Three people have been arrested.
Indian cinema abroad | Two Indian films have been selected for the Busan International film festival, which begins on 6 October. Birds in the Dark, by Shashank Walia, explores an unexpected human connection while Tamil writer-director Sailesh Rathnakumar’s Selvi is set in the world of home-care workers.
Guest shelf
A recommendation from someone with great taste
Photographer Aashim Tyagi (@aashim), who once documented Art Deco architecture in Gujarat’s Balasinor, suggests a prehistoric side quest: “I was intrigued by the town’s reputation as the ‘Jurassic Park of India’ and a little digging led me to a dinosaur museum in neighbouring Raiyoli. It’s set amid open fields near one of Asia’s largest fossil beds where Rajasaurus narmadensis and a dozen other species once roamed. Much of the museum and the village’s paleontological preservation is owed to Aaliya Babi of Balasinor’s erstwhile royal family, earning her the nickname ‘Dinosaur Princess’. Balasinor and its dinosaur museum are a worthwhile detour from Ahmedabad or Baroda.”
Count it
A number worth knowing
176
India ranked 176th, second from the bottom, in the 2026 Environmental Performance Index, which evaluates countries on environmental health, climate change and ecosystem vitality. The country recorded negative values on air-quality indicators but showed an improvement on the index’s 10-year change metric. In 2022, when India had been ranked last, the central government had dismissed the EPI’s conclusions, saying it used “unscientific methods”.

title: The Nepal and Tibet flood is a warning: melting snow and ice will bring more disasters around the world
text:
You may not have felt it, but the earth beneath our feet is getting twitchier, and global heating is to blame. As temperatures surge and climate breakdown accelerates, interactions between climate and geology are becoming ever more apparent – as marked by last week’s horrific events in Nepal and Tibet. We still have a bit of a blind spot when it comes to the idea that a changing climate can impact what scientists call the geosphere, but the evidence has long been incontestable.
In 2021, a similar deluge ripped through a series of mountain valleys in the Indian Himalayan state of Uttarakhand, severely damaging two hydroelectric power plants and taking about 200 lives. In August 2025, a colossal landslide in an Alaskan fjord created a 500-metre-high wave in an area frequented by cruise ships. A few months earlier, the collapse of part of a glacier in Switzerland’s Valais canton caused a debris-laden torrent that destroyed and buried most of the already evacuated village of Blatten.
What all four events have in common is that they involve what is known as the cryosphere – the sum total of the planet’s frozen water. The fact that ice, snow and permafrost are severely affected by global heating should come as no surprise, and this means that the poles and high mountain regions are bearing the brunt. Everywhere, the cryosphere is receding rapidly, and this is bad news.
As glaciers retreat, they expose unstable terrain that is often ripe for landslides. The swift thawing of permafrost as global heating causes freezing levels to progressively rise also means that mountain faces become unstable rock masses looking for any excuse to collapse. At the same time, wherever there is an available dip or hollow, glacial meltwater is accumulating, forming expanding lakes that are increasingly prone to overtopping or breaching, dumping prodigious volumes of water into inhabited valleys downslope.
In such circumstances, there are manifold ways in which climate-driven responses from the earth under our feet can drive dangerous and deadly hazards. As in Nepal and Tibet, the collapse of a weakened glacier can promote a flood, either directly, or by throwing a dam across a river valley that is eventually breached. Permafrost thawing, heavy rains or an earthquake can lead to the formation of landslides that can also block rivers, or obliterate communities completely.
In Alaska – one of the fastest-heating places on the planet – the loss of huge amounts of ice has reduced the load on active faults in the crust beneath, and is facilitating earthquake activity. A similar seismic backlash can be expected in other rapidly melting icy strongholds, including the Himalayas, the Andes, Greenland, and perhaps also the European Alps. Ice melt-related quakes have themselves the potential to provoke devastating landslides or glacier collapses, and to cause the breaching of meltwater lakes, resulting in what are known as glacial lake outburst floods. These will become increasingly common as more water from melting ice and snow accumulates at high altitudes. There are thousands of glacial lakes across the Himalayan region alone, about 200 of which have been diagnosed as presenting a threat to communities downslope.
There is no question that high mountain communities sit on the frontline of climate breakdown, but it would be a mistake to think that the planet isn’t getting jittery elsewhere, too. The reality is that the geosphere is extraordinarily sensitive, so that a tiny change in environmental conditions can result in a potentially hazardous geological response.
This is why there is actually a volcano “season” – more eruptions happen between November and April than at other times of the year, promoted by minute-scale deformation of the Earth’s crust linked to an annual redistribution of water mass around the planet. It’s why a seismologist colleague of mine is fond of warning that if a dangerous earthquake fault is locked and loaded, it can be triggered by just the same pressure as you’d apply in a handshake. What this all means is that a minuscule variation in some environmental metric – be it air pressure, crustal stress, precipitation, sea level or ice load – can provide the final straw that prompts a geological reaction.
Add in the fact that environmental parameters such as temperature, precipitation and sea levels are all on the rise, and you have that extra nudge that can goad an inactive volcano into erupting, cause a long-dormant fault to rupture, or coax the snout of an unstable glacier to collapse. The end product can be a devastating geological event that is out of all proportion to the size of the initial trigger.
There are places that have historically been geologically quiet where a heating climate is likely to result in an awakening. Greenland is ground zero in this regard. Here, the weight of the ice cover, at 2km to 3km thick, has meant that any faults beneath have not been able to move for thousands of years. Now, though, the ice is melting and the load on the faults is reducing. A future rise in earthquake activity is predicted as a consequence.
Iceland is also worth keeping an eye on. There, the reduced load arising from the rapid retreat of the Vatnajökull ice sheet is forecast to increase activity from volcanoes lurking beneath. The huge impact on aviation of the 2010 eruption of Eyjafjallajökull provides us with some inkling of the chaos this could bring to the UK and northern Europe.
The increasingly temperamental behaviour of the earth beneath our feet teaches us that global heating is all-pervasive. It will intrude into every aspect of our lives and livelihoods, and leave no part of the planet untouched. As the world processes the horror of the events in Nepal and Tibet, it is a lesson that we ignore at our peril.
- 
  Bill McGuire is professor emeritus of geophysical and climate hazards at UCL. His latest book is The Fate of the World – a History and Future of the Climate Crisis

title: Remote Grand Canyon lodge hit by deadly flash flood boasts fabled history
text:
Phantom Ranch has been a solitary refuge visited by some of the most famous names of history. More typically, it’s been a beacon for more than a century for the half-collapsed, exhausted and overheated hikers trudging down the Grand Canyon.
The sole lodge at the very bottom of the Grand Canyon, the cabins long had a near mythical reputation. Located along the Bright Angel Creek, which tumbles into the mighty Colorado River at the base of the canyon, they served as a reminder of the long history of one of America’s most spectacular but savage environments.
It’s unclear yet how much damage the lodge has sustained after Saturday’s lethal flash flood.
On Saturday afternoon, more than 60 people had to be evacuated by air from the ranch and the bottom of the adjacent North Kaibab Trail, which winds 14 miles down from the lesser-trodden North Rim of the canyon. Two people were confirmed dead, nearly 80 people were rescued and one person remained unaccounted for.
Native Americans have made their home in various parts of the canyon for thousands of years and were driven out of much – though not all – of it before President Theodore Roosevelt declared the canyon a national monument in 1908. It was Roosevelt who set up a camp on the site where the little visitor lodge now stands, while he was on a hunting trip in 1913. The area became a national park in 1919 and the ranch, named after one of the many side canyons within the Grand Canyon, opened in 1922.
Boaters floating and paddling down the Colorado River stay there, as do people riding mules. The future King Gustaf VI Adolf of Sweden was a prominent early guest, arriving via mule, in 1926.
In 1967, then senator Robert F Kennedy stayed at Phantom Ranch beneath the towering canyon walls after rafting down the Colorado with family and friends, bouncing and gliding 90 miles on the east-west flow of the river from Lake Powell.
Today, more than a vertical mile above, the hundreds of thousands of visitors who just peep over the South Rim, where lodges, tourist information spots, shops and restaurants buzz, cannot see the river, let alone the tiny ranch so far below.
But hikers who trek down the seven or eight zigzag miles of the nearby dusty South Kaibab or Bright Angel trails to the bottom and cross footbridges over the Colorado to reach the ranch descend steadily from tourist hullabaloo into an ever more rugged and tranquil wilderness. Here, heat, thirst or flood are the biggest dangers, not the resident mountain lions, rattlesnakes or scorpions.
Having pounded the hard rock paths and rough steps all the way down, the few who get to stay at the ranch or snag a campsite along the creek are mostly thinking of the relief of not having to climb back up to the rim yet and the magic of cooling their throbbing feet in a stream before a simple canteen meal at communal tables and a rudimentary bed for a night or two.
But that sense of safety can be as elusively spectral as the name of the refuge. A fast and fierce deluge, such as occurred at the weekend, can quickly form a roaring flash flood when the rain swells creeks that drop steeply into the canyon as tributaries to the Colorado, which is what just happened in the Bright Angel Creek.
The National Park Service describes flash flooding as an inherent risk in the canyon but had additionally warned in February of “the elevated potential for flash flooding and debris flows in the Bright Angel Creek watershed” following the Dragon Bravo wildfire that decimated parts of the North Rim last year and forced the closure of the North Kaibab trail from July to March of this year.

title: Two people dead and nearly 80 rescued after Grand Canyon flash flood
text:
A second death was confirmed by National Park Service officials on Monday after a flash flood sent a surge of water and debris through an area of the Grand Canyon over the weekend.
Dozens of visitors had to be evacuated by helicopter during the deluge, which consumed trails and infrastructure. Nearly 80 people were rescued and one person is still unaccounted for, as more heavy rain and thunderstorms in the forecasts threaten additional debris flows, flash floods or rock falls, the NPS said in a statement.
“With deep monsoonal moisture in place and already saturated soils in some locations, an elevated risk of flash flooding will be in place through Monday,” the National Weather Service (NWS) said.
Incident commander Dave Black said officials used night-vision and other equipment to find people who needed to be evacuated over the weekend.
Park officials called on the public to provide any information on those who may have been hiking or backpacking in the inner canyon near Bright Angel Creek, or campers with a reservation in the area.
Flash floods are not uncommon in the region, especially during the monsoon season from June to September when strong rains pummel the arid landscapes and can quickly fill narrow rock formations. Visiting the Grand Canyon – a crown jewel of the US national park system – can be particularly dangerous in the summer because of the risk of flash flooding that accompanies the monsoon, when clear days can give way quickly to thunderstorms and downpours.
The deluge that unleashed torrents of rain on hardened and sparsely vegetated steep terrain came as the Grand Canyon region – and the Colorado River basin that runs through it – continue to be mired in a severe drought that has fueled a widespread water crisis.
Scientists have long warned that the climate crisis will create stronger extremes and destructive shifts between wet and dry conditions. The sudden and strong rainstorm that fueled this catastrophic flood may have been been supercharged by the historic El Niño that has sharply increased sea surface temperatures in the Pacific Ocean, which has the ability to affect weather systems around the world.
The NWS has issued flood watches across a large part of the south-west, including in northern Arizona. Officials cautioned against visiting creeks, slot canyons, burn scars and low water crossings in the area, where flash floods can quickly develop.
Videos taken by hikers before they were airlifted to safety showed churning brown waters carrying large metal objects and other debris. Some crossed the bridges just shortly before they were consumed by the waterway.
“It must have been, like, 10 minutes afterwards – we crossed the bridges to get to the evacuation zone,” hiker Gabriel Burgeman told a local news station. “We were just barely in time to cross them before they got wiped out.”
The body of a 46-year-old man was recovered on Sunday evening near Crystal Rapids along the Colorado River, the NPS said, without providing additional details. At least one other body has been recovered, according to a statement posted on Facebook by the Grand Canyon national park without details.
Early assessments also showed roughly 40% of a key pipeline that provides drinking water for tourists and residents had been damaged or destroyed. The 12.5-mile (20km) Transcanyon Waterline has endured dozens of breaks in recent years. A more than $200m repair and replacement project was well under way when the floods hit.
The pipeline moves water from one side of the canyon, down to its base, across a bridge and back up the other side of the rough landscape. Any effort to fix a break from rock falls or flash floods is time-consuming, precarious and costly, so addressing the latest damage will be complicated.
Emergency water restrictions began on Monday, closing down all overnight stay lodges and hotels within Grand Canyon national park, and spigots at campgrounds on the South Rim were turned off. Year-round residents were asked to conserve water. The park had water conservation measures in place even before the latest bout of flooding and damage.
The flooding on Saturday in Bright Angel Creek, which flows into the river, led to more than 60 people being airlifted from the canyon’s depths.
Parth Desai was hiking through a narrow passage in Bright Angel Canyon with fellow physicians and a park ranger when heavy rain started falling on Saturday.
“We saw the creek flood, waterfalls coming up out of nowhere, boulders, mud, landslides happening everywhere,” he said.
Torrents of water wiped out footbridges over the creek and altered the landscape, widening the creek bed and extending an existing river rapid or creating a new one. The flood was a blow to an enduring effort to modernize the pipeline that serves 6 million visitors a year and roughly 1,600 residents of Grand Canyon Village.
“Heaven help us if the whole thing down there at the bottom has to be reconstructed,” said Jack Schmidt, director of the Center for Colorado River Studies at Utah State University. “Where are they going to get the money?”
Halting overnight stays at the park because of a lack of water is rare, although the pipeline frequently has failed over the years. While the Grand Canyon has large storage tanks for potable water on the South Rim, they will not be refilled while the pipeline is out of service.
A $208m rehabilitation of the pipeline and upgrades to the associated water delivery system started in 2023, with the park service calling it a crucial investment to ensure the park can meet the needs of residents and visitors. The project was expected to be completed next year.
In unrelated flooding, officials in San Antonio, Texas, on Sunday reported a pair of deaths related to a severe storm there two days earlier.
Police said a 46-year-old woman died after being caught in rushing water in San Pedro Creek north of downtown, Texas Public Radio reported. A person with that woman escaped safely, police said.
Separately, police said a man in his 50s was found at Woodlawn Park on Sunday morning.
The woman’s death is being investigated as a drowning while the man’s death is considered a possible drowning, police said.
The Associated Press contributed reporting
