text:
- 
  Rescue teams rushed into action after flooding and landslides caused by a “glacial collapse” at the China-Nepal border left hundreds of people dead or missing. Officials in Nepal said on Thursday that more than 400 tourists were among those unaccounted for, including many foreign nationals, while China reported more than 500 people missing including more than 250 foreigners.
- 
  Surveillance video from the Chinese side of the border showed a huge wave of mud and debris crashing over a building several storeys high, engulfing it as dozens of people fled for their lives below. The surge swept away buses and cars. Other videos showed entire towns and their surrounds wiped out as the muddy flood rushed down the mountain slopes and along populated valleys.
- 
  An earthquake was initially thought to be the cause; but by Thursday the US Geological Survey (USGS) said “a glacial collapse” was responsible for the disaster. “This event was initially reported as a magnitude 4.4 earthquake. Additional analysis of nearby seismic stations, long period seismic waves, and satellite imagery led to the determination that the seismic event was instead a glacial collapse and debris flow, and that no earthquake had occurred.” The USGS first reported the seismic jolt early on Wednesday about 66km (41 miles) north of Kathmandu, near the border.
- 
  Entire villages and markets were “wiped out”, the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies said. It was dispatching emergency supplies including blankets, first aid kits, stretchers and body bags. The United Nations secretary general, António Guterres, said UN teams and partners were mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support affected communities.
- 
  Experts warned that a lingering blockage upstream on the Nepal-China border river could produce a second flood.
- 
  Nepal’s tourism ministry said the missing included scores of Indian nationals, Britons, Americans, Australians and Canadians as well as others from South Korea, the Netherlands, Malaysia, Portugal and South Africa. At least 28 Nepalese police were missing, a police spokesperson said.
- 
  By evening local time on Thursday in Nepal, police said the death toll was at more than 350, with more than 800 missing. There were at least three dead and 558 missing in Tibet, an autonomous region of China, authorities said
-

title: Girl, 13, among missing British citizens after flash flood in Nepal
text:
Thirty-three British citizens including a 13-year-old girl are among more than 400 travellers missing after a flash flood on the Nepal-Tibet border, according to Nepal’s tourism board.
The sudden flood happened on the Tibetan side of the Bhote Koshi River at about 8.30am local time on Wednesday. The 33 UK citizens are among at least 341 foreign nationals unaccounted for.
Earlier on Wednesday, the tour operator Alpine Eco Trek said a 13-year-old girl was among the missing British nationals, with two Irish citizens also missing.
Among the missing British nationals are three men aged 65, 64 and 52, and seven women aged 44, 47, 51, 60, 63, 63 and 65, according to travel logs.
The firm, which offers guided tours and expeditions in Nepal, confirmed four of its Nepali tour guides – aged 38, 35, 45 and 29 – are missing as well.
Kumar Adhikari, the manager of Alpine Eco Trek, said on Wednesday: “I feel so sad. We are just thinking about what to do next.
“We are in pain at the moment, deep pain.”
Adhikari said the tour group, who were on a nine-day tour to Mount Kailash, were crossing into Tibet from Nepal when they became trapped at the border as the flash floods struck.
He said he was in contact with his tour guides until 8.40am when their phones went offline, at which point the group would have been inside Tibet’s immigration office.
“We were hoping that inside it was safe,” he said. “But later the video came from China’s government which (showed) even Tibet’s side was hit by the flood.”
The tourist board said more than 100 of the missing people were yet to have a nationality confirmed.
Police in Nepal said 157 bodies had been recovered and more than 40 people were injured and receiving treatment in hospital.
A wall of mud and rock appeared to have collapsed into the river on the Himalayan border of Nepal and Tibet, triggering catastrophic flooding on the Nepali side, Reuters reported. It said verified videos showed dozens of people being swept away at the border.
Houses, roads and energy infrastructure were destroyed in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties”, with some people missing in the county of Gyirong after a mudslide hit a border land crossing.
Initial reports suggested an earthquake had triggered an avalanche and caused the floods, Shisir Khanal, Nepal’s foreign minister, told the country’s parliament.
Eight South Koreans working on a hydropower plant were missing and 10 others stranded, South Korea’s foreign ministry said.
Local authorities said tourists in the Rasuwa district of Nepal and other areas along the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers should “exercise extreme caution”, remain in safe areas and move to higher ground if required.
Visitors were urged to stay in regular contact with hotels and travel agencies. People planning to travel to the affected areas in the coming days were warned to postpone their journeys.
The UK’s foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, said: “I am deeply concerned to hear of the flash floods on the Nepal-China border. All my thoughts are with those affected and with British nationals in the area and their relatives here at home.”
The British embassy in Kathmandu urged people in affected areas to follow local advice. A joint statement with the embassies of Australia, the EU, Finland, France, Norway and Switzerland said: “We are deeply saddened by the devastating flooding in Rasuwa and Nuwakot districts and surrounding areas. Our thoughts are with all those affected by this disaster. We express our solidarity with the people of Nepal during this difficult time.
“We encourage all those in affected areas to follow the guidance of local authorities and official safety advisories as the situation continues to evolve.”

title: Flash floods on Nepal-Tibet border leave scores dead and hundreds missing
text:
At least 157 people have been killed and hundreds, including large numbers of foreign tourists, are missing after flash floods hit the Himalayan border areas of Nepal and Tibet in China, police have said, with parts of India also at risk.
The disaster was caused by a torrent of mud, water and debris that burst from the banks of a river that runs between China and Nepal. Homes, roads, bridges and power plants were swept away in Nepal, while officials in Tibet said they feared “major casualties”.
The US Geological Survey initially reported the event as a 4.4-magnitude earthquake, but additional analysis indicated the “seismic energy was instead generated by a glacial collapse and debris flow”.
Authorities issued alerts urging residents in several districts to avoid the Bhote Koshi, Trishuli and Narayani rivers in Nepal.
Officials in Nepal said 403 people, including 341 from foreign countries including India, the US, the UK, Australia, South Korea and Malaysia, had been reported missing in the country.
Nepal’s tourism board said more than 100 of those missing were religious tourists from India and the Indian diaspora on a pilgrimage to Mount Kailash in Tibet, a sacred site for Hindus. At least 62 missing Nepali citizens were among hundreds of locals trekking in Rasuwa, one of the worst hit districts.
The board said that 47 of the missing tourists were from the United States, 34 from Australia, 33 from Britain and 24 from Canada. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said UN teams and partners were mobilising supplies and personnel in Nepal to support communities affected by the disaster.
In Tibet, China’s state broadcaster said at least three people were killed and 265 were missing.
Officials said the flooding could get worse because parts of the river remained blocked by ice rocks and debris.
Flood alerts were also issued in the Indian states of Bihar and Uttar Pradesh, which border Nepal and are downstream of the affected rivers.
Police in Nepal said they were still unable to assess the full scale of the damage. Rescuers said helicopters could not land in affected areas of Syapru Besi and Timure in the mountainous district of Rasuwa until the river waters had receded. Rescue efforts were also hampered by heavy monsoon rains.
Images of crumbled homes in the flood waters, floating cars and a metal bridge being washed away, and villages engulfed by water, mud and debris were broadcast on Nepali television.
“There could be heavy casualties or loss of property,” said the district administrator, Narendra Pariyar, who urged those living on the banks of the Bhote Koshi to move to higher ground.
“There is devastation everywhere we look,” said Tula Bahadur BK, a health worker in Rasuwa. “The settlements next to the river have been completely swept away. Five of my own relatives are missing.”
Nepal’s energy ministry said the country’s electricity supplies had been significantly affected, mostly as a result of destroyed hydroelectric plants.
Police and military officers joined in Nepal’s rescue effort, the country’s prime minister, Balendra Shah, said. “Instructions have been given … to move the people living in the lower areas to safer places. People along the river are advised to exercise extra caution and remain alert.”
The Indian prime minister, Narendra Modi, said he had spoken with Shah and offered Nepal “all possible types of humanitarian assistance”.
China’s official Xinhua news agency said the flash flood occurred on the Nepal side of the border and cut roads, communications and power links in the Shigatse region.
Chinese authorities were conducting large-scale search and rescue operations in the Tibetan border area of Gyirong, according to state broadcaster CCTV.
China’s president, Xi Jinping, urged “all-out” search efforts for the missing and better monitoring and early warning systems to prevent secondary disasters.
The Himalayan region, which spans Nepal, India, China and Bhutan, is particularly vulnerable to floods and landslides because it is warming faster than the rest of the world as a result of the climate crisis.
Research shows that extreme weather events such as heatwaves and torrential rains have become more frequent. Nepal’s snow-capped mountains had lost close to one-third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global warming, the United Nations said in 2023. Experts have called for greater surveillance and early warning systems across the Himalayan region.
Last year, a flood from the Bhote Koshi River killed nine people and washed away a “friendship bridge” linking Nepal and China, disrupting trade and transport for months.
Researchers in Kathmandu also found earlier this year that glaciers across the Hindu Kush region were melting at an accelerating rate. Ice loss rates have doubled since 2000.

title: Typhoon Narra: record flood waters submerge homes and force mass evacuations in China
text:
Widespread flooding triggered by Typhoon Narra has submerged homes and forced mass evacuations in southern China, as another storm system tracked towards Japan and Taiwan.
Authorities in Chongzuo, in China’s Guangxi region – famous for its giant waterfalls and karst limestone mountains – on Tuesday evacuated more than 15,000 people after water levels surpassed a record high set in 2008.
Rising flood waters have prompted China to relocate a total of 54,000 people in Guangxi, state television said.
Narra made landfall as a tropical storm on Tuesday evening in China’s southern island province of Hainan after lingering over the Beibu Gulf for several days, dumping heavy rain on Guangxi, Hainan and Guangdong.
Heavy rain is expected to persist across parts of Vietnam and southern China through Wednesday, with areas of Guangxi, Guangdong, Hainan and Fujian forecast to receive torrential rain, state media said.
In Chongzuo, river water overflowed into the city, with water levels reaching the rooftops of some buildings and power lines.
A notice from Chongzuo authorities on Monday ordered all businesses and tourist operations to cease and urged evacuated residents not to return to high-risk areas.
Meanwhile, medium-strength Typhoon Saudel moved towards southern Japan and northern Taiwan where it is expected to bring sporadic heavy rain, as Taiwan reported one dead and four missing from a separate weather system over its south and east.
Japan’s weather agency warned of destructive winds and high seas as Typhoon Saudel approached the south-western islands of Okinawa prefecture.
Saudel is expected to pass to the north of Taiwan starting late Thursday and into Friday, though its intensity is forecast to gradually weaken, the island’s Central Weather Administration said.
However, there is uncertainty about the timing and extent of the typhoon’s rainfall impact, it added.
In southern and eastern Taiwan, the government reported one person dead and four missing from a tropical depression that brought flooding in the cities of Tainan and Kaohsiung, home to more than 4 million people.
During the three days from Sunday to Tuesday, almost a metre (3.9 feet) of rain fell in Kaohsiung, which the government said exceeded rainfall during 2009’s devastating Typhoon Morakot that killed about 700 people and caused damage of up to $3bn.
Saudel is forecast to hit the coast in the south-eastern Chinese province of Fujian from late Thursday to early Friday.

title: Weather tracker: Tornadoes cause flash flooding and power cuts in north-east US
text:
Thunderstorms and tornadoes caused damage and disruption last Thursday as severe weather hit the US north-east. A tornado struck Dover, Delaware, with another reported near Atlantic Beach on Long Island in New York.
The latter was rated EF-1 by the National Weather Service, with peak winds of 97mph (156kph). It was the first tornado reported in Nassau County since November 2021, with buildings and beach cabanas damaged, and heavy rainfall causing flash flooding and power cuts.
In the UK, after a summer of high temperatures and virtually no meaningful rainfall it has turned cooler over recent days, with the arrival of some heavy showers and thunderstorms. High pressure brought a mainly dry and settled weekend, but more unsettled weather will arrive from Tuesday. Showers, thunderstorms and longer spells of thundery rain are expected to spread northwards, with temperatures increasing as warmer southerly winds develop.
Meanwhile, a powerful El Niño is developing in the Pacific Ocean and could be the strongest in living memory, according to the UK Met Office. El Niño is a naturally occurring climate pattern that occurs every two to seven years. It can trigger major shifts in global weather, leading to drought, flooding and wildfires but no two events are the same and the impacts from one event to the other can be different. The effects are greatest in the tropics. India has already experienced weaker than average monsoon rainfall, while hurricane activity in the Atlantic has been suppressed.
Trade winds that usually move from east to west across the Pacific Ocean can weaken or even reverse, allowing warm water to push eastwards. Sea surface temperatures in the region are forecast to climb by more than 3C above average later this year, which would make it the strongest El Niño since records began in 1950. Some forecasts suggest it could reach an unprecedented 4C above average. Global temperatures rise due to the transfer of heat from the ocean to the atmosphere, and this year’s El Niño means that 2027 is likely to be the warmest year ever recorded globally.
For the UK, El Niño increases the risk of a wet and stormy autumn. It can also increase the risk of colder weather developing later in the winter across north-west Europe. There are already signs in some of the longer-range forecast models that this autumn and the early part of winter could be wetter than normal. In a warming world, the impacts of El Niño are likely to be more severe, but there is currently no strong evidence that climate change is making these events more likely.

title: Tornadoes pummel New Yorkâs Long Island and Delaware capital
text:
Residents in Delaware’s capital and on Long Island, New York, were picking up the pieces on Friday after tornadoes touched down during sudden storms that battered the north-eastern US with heavy rains and left dozens of people stranded in their cars during flash flooding.
In Atlantic Beach on Long Island, images posted on social media showed a large funnel cloud over the water and small buildings torn apart at a beach club.
A tornado touched down at the Sun & Surf Beach Club, leaving one person with minor injuries and major damage to at least 50 beach cabanas, according to the Nassau county chief fire marshal, Michael Uttaro.
The beach club was hosting a party with between 200 and 300 people when the storm hit and club members had started to evacuate before the tornado struck, fire officials told Newsday.
The Sun & Surf and Silver Point, another affected club, said they will be closed until further notice as damage is assessed.
The National Weather Service said a trained spotter also reported a tornado in Dover, Delaware, during Thursday evening’s storms. Pictures and video on social media show the roof of a motel being blown off and damage to other buildings along Route 13 north-east of downtown.
The mayor of Dover, Robin Christiansen, said a state of emergency was lifted on Friday morning to allow residents and businesses to resume normal activities. Police urged residents to be patient and set aside extra time for travel.
“There is still debris throughout the city, and crews will be out working on cleanup, repairs, and restoring services. You may encounter blocked lanes, utility crews, emergency personnel, and other delays,” local police said on social media.
Back in Long Island, the Nassau county executive, Bruce Blakeman, said first responders rescued people trapped in their vehicles during flooding.
In other parts of New York, flooding caused part of the Long Island Expressway in the borough of Queens to close in both directions, according to New York City emergency management. Photos on social media showed lines of stopped cars as emergency crews traversed the water.
In Jersey City, New Jersey, emergency crews rescued 69 people trapped in cars that were overtaken by flash flooding, said the mayor, James Solomon. Emergency crews used small inflatable boats to reach people who were stranded.
Tornadoes are relatively rare in the US north-east compared with the country’s interior.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: Food security is an issue we can no longer ignore
text:
George Monbiot is right that Britain has become dangerously complacent about food security (Britain’s scorched fields mean a food crisis – and the government is ignoring the one measure that would help, 13 August). A country facing climate shocks, disrupted trade routes and increasingly volatile harvests – all of which contribute to not only the availability of food but its increased cost – cannot rely indefinitely on just-in-time supply chains and supermarket logistics.
But strategic food reserves are only part of the answer. The other underused resource is our communities themselves. Research has shown that during floods, infrastructure failures and other emergencies, local groups, charities and neighbours are often the real first responders, stepping in long before formal systems can fully mobilise. Resilience is not just about what sits in a warehouse; it is about the strength of local networks, trusted relationships and the capacity of people to act together.
That is why food security should also be seen as a question of land use and reciprocal trust. Councils, NHS bodies, universities and other public institutions hold significant areas of underused land that could support community food-growing, local skills and stronger neighbourhood connections. Brilliant organisations such as Incredible Edible have proved this model can – and does – work. This land can and should become civic infrastructure for food, nature and belonging.
The lesson of recent crises is not limited to questions about government stockpiling of food; it should also be about investing in building the long-term sustainable community capacity that helps people withstand shocks together.
Dan Farag
Director of innovation and practice, The Young Foundation
George Monbiot accuses the British government of complacency over national food security. By coincidence, on the day his article appeared, the UN publicised the recently released 86-page report Roadmap for Resilience: A UK Food Plan for 2050 by UK Research and Innovation.
This detailed document provides foresight-based assessments of the national food situation and offers a palette of solutions to the problem of food security, supported by a significant amount of research. Interestingly, it does not mention stockpiling, Monbiot’s suggested solution. Hence there seems to be a divergence of opinions on strategy.
Government bodies in the UK have been working on food security issues for decades. The silence of elected representatives is enigmatic because we don’t know whether they have shelved the problem or simply left it to civil servants and researchers to deal with. A more open debate, led by politicians, would help us assess whether the Food Plan for 2050 is wishful thinking or the answer to the problem, and whether stockpiling of food is likely to be any use.
David E Alexander
Emeritus professor of emergency planning and management, UCL
George Monbiot is right that Britain needs to take food security much more seriously, but stockpiling should be understood as part of a wider resilience strategy.
Switzerland offers a useful example. Its national economic supply system requires the private sector to maintain stocks of essential foodstuffs, amounting to several months’ supply. Crucially, it also provides for stocks of agricultural inputs, including fertilisers. This recognises that if a crisis extends from weeks into whole growing seasons, national food security depends on being able to produce the next harvest.
However, stockpiles can only go so far. A government can pre-emptively fill silos with grain and still watch its population go hungry if electricity grids collapse or fuel supplies are severed. Food security ultimately depends on the complex web of energy, transport, water, communications and other infrastructure.
Britain should therefore ask not simply how much food we should stockpile, but what capabilities we need to preserve to keep people fed when the next crisis lasts longer than expected.
Antony So
Contributor, Just in Case: Narrowing the Civil Food Resilience Gap, National Preparedness Commission

title: Hawaii crews work to restore power to thousands after Lala outages
text:
Crews in Hawaii are working to restore power to thousands of residents after the outer bands of Hurricane Lala battered the islands over the weekend, causing destructive flooding and killing one person.
On the hard-hit Big Island, crews were working to clear and restore roads, but some communities on the southern end of the island remained isolated as they were cut off from communication.
Hawaiian Electric said inspections were showing significant damage across the island group, especially in remote areas. Crews were working overnight to restore power to thousands across the Big Island, Maui and Oahu.
Most public schools reopened but Hawaii county’s non-emergency operations were still suspended, officials said.
Officials said the storm caused one death – a 90-year-old woman who had been reported missing in Naalehu and then found dead on Monday.
Lala blew past the Hawaiian islands on Saturday. The hurricane had weakened to a tropical storm, but still brought significant damage to homes, roads and bridges.
Hawaii’s governor, Josh Green, said on Monday that the damage was not as catastrophic as feared and that recovery would be “somewhat brisk”.
The storm has since moved west, according to the National Weather Service. It is expected to eventually turn north toward the Papahānaumokuākea Marine national monument, a vast and remote federally protected area of the Pacific with islands, atolls, sea mounts, shoals and coral reefs.

title: South Korea city deluged by almost a metre of rain, triggering deadly landslide
text:
Torrential downpours that pounded southern parts of South Korea since Saturday have killed one person and injured four others, officials have confirmed.
Heavy rains have been recorded in South Gyeongsang province, including the city of Geoje, where an 800mm (31in) deluge over the weekend triggered a landslide, the interior and safety ministry said. The rain continued on Monday, bringing the cumulative rainfall total to 912mm by 6pm.
Police and firefighters rescued three residents from an apartment building hit by the landslide, but one of them was found in cardiac arrest and was later pronounced dead at a hospital, according to Yonhap.
Two people were injured in Geoje and two others in nearby cities, the ministry said.
Geoje received 805.7mm of rain from Saturday through to 8am on Monday, Yonhap reported, while the neighbouring city of Tongyeong received 671.9mm during the same period. Other parts of the province received between 240mm and 340mm of rain.
The heavy rains that have pummelled southern South Korea since Saturday have triggered warnings from authorities, forced about 390 people to evacuate and caused power outages at about 3,580 houses.
The Korea Herald quoted weather officials on Tuesday as saying that South Gyeongsang province had received an entire summer’s rainfall in just two days, with record daily rainfall totals in the two cities of Geoje and Tongyeong.
Twelve schools and kindergartens have reportedly flooded, while firefighters have received dozens of calls from residents seeking help with rain related damage and accidents, authorities said.
Prime minister Han Seong-sook also instructed police, firefighters and other authorities to make every effort to rescue stranded residents and others at risk from the heavy rain.
Heavy monsoon rains have also flooded key streets and snarled traffic in the Philippine capital, Manila, with the government on Monday suspending government work and asking schools to shift to online learning.
About three weeks of intermittent monsoon rains and a storm that lashed the main northern island region of Luzon two weeks ago left at least 23 people dead, mostly due to landslides and floods, and affected 5 million people, including nearly 25,000, who remained in government emergency shelters on Monday in several northern provinces, according to the office of civil defence.
Among the dead were 10 people, including children, whose houses were buried by an 9 August landslide in the northern mountain resort city of Baguio. Three others were dug out alive with injuries by rescuers from the avalanche of mud, rocks and debris that collapsed from a mountainside as people slept, officials said.
With Associated Press

title: Lala weakens to tropical storm as it lashes Hawaii with heavy wind and rain
text:
Hurricane Lala weakened to a tropical storm on Sunday after skirting Hawaii without making landfall, but it wasn’t done punishing the Big Island with hurricane-force gusts. Total rainfall of nearly 3ft (1 meter) was expected on the higher windward slopes, turning rivers into raging torrents and threatening mudslides.
The Hawaii governor, Josh Green, said at least one person died in a car accident in the South Point area of the Big Island, where more than 100 homes were destroyed. A little over 183,000 utility customers remained without power across Hawaii by Sunday mid-afternoon, according to the utility tracker PowerOutage.us. At least three hospitals were operating on generator power, and 19 roofs were lost, Green said.
A search-and-rescue mission including civil defense, the national guard and coast guard was launched after flash floods apparently swept several occupied homes off their foundations in the coastal communities of Na’alehu and Wai’ohinu, near the island’s southern tip, the Hawaii county mayor, Kimo Alameda, said early on Sunday.
“You definitely want to be home, do not be out on the roads,” said Green, who had earlier described Lala as an “enormous storm”.
Tropical storm conditions were spreading westward on Sunday from Maui to Oahu and then Kauai, and the National Hurricane Center warned that wind speeds atop mountains and on the windward and leeward slopes are often up to 30% stronger than the near-surface winds used to categorize storms.
The possibility the island could witness its first direct hit from a hurricane in 155 years faded as the eye of the storm passed the island’s southern tip. Landfall was not expected at this point, said the National Weather Service (NWS) meteorologist Joseph Clark.
However, hurricane-force winds were expected to continue into the overnight hours, with the strongest wind gusts likely in areas of higher terrain, the National Hurricane Center said. Heavy rainfall into Sunday could produce flooding and mudslides, while powerful waves pound the coast, the agency said.
Tropical storm warnings remained in effect for the islands of Molokai, Lanai, Kahoolawe, Kauai and Niihau as the storm moved west, raising the possibility of destructive flooding and even wildfires kicked up by strong winds.
The beloved Punalu’u Bake Shop in Naalehu, Big Island, a tourist hotspot and major local employer, was severely damaged. Zachary Kennedy, the manager of the Hawaiian sweet bread bakery, said water rushed through their factories and retail store, leaving behind about 3ft of mud.
“This is a different level of damage. It’s literally catastrophic,” Kennedy said.
Forecasters said higher elevations on the island, dominated by the towering Mauna Kea volcano, could get as much as 35in (89cm) of rain. That could cause life-threatening mudslides where some of Big Island’s 210,000 residents live off the grid in improvised housing.
As the hurricane approached, shelters were opened, events were canceled and ranchers were urged to leave their cattle in pastures rather than structures that might collapse. Many residents are still dealing with the aftermath of devastating floods in March and were taking precautions.
Bobby Camara, a 75-year-old lifelong resident, said he planned to “hunker down, cross my fingers, [and] hope the lights don’t go out” at a care home just outside Hilo. He said gas stations were busy as people sought fuel for chainsaws and vehicles.
“I think stocking up is part of life over here,” Camara said. “You learn to be self-reliant.”
Mike Caputo, who lives in Keaau, near the Big Island’s east coast, said his power generator was ready and a 10,000-gallon (37.8 kiloliter) home water tank was full. He said the main concern was flash flooding and fallen trees, especially albizia, a common tree.
“They’re not very sturdy, but they grow extremely large,” said Caputo, 50, a local fire captain. “They can make roads impassable.”
Lala intensified from a tropical storm into a hurricane early Saturday as its maximum sustained winds increased to 75mph (120km/h), the hurricane center reported, making it a category 1 hurricane.
A hurricane last made landfall on the islands in 1992, when Hurricane Iniki – a category 4 storm – lashed Kauai.
The Big Island was last hit directly in 1871, when a category 3 hurricane hit the north-east corner, according to research by a University of Hawaii atmospheric scientist.
The hurricane center predicted 8-12in (20.3-30.5cm) of total rainfall across Maui and the lower elevations of the Big Island, and 4-6in (10.2-15.2cm) across the island chain.

title: Torrential rain and flood kill nine in Japan amid wettest month in decades
text:
Heavy rain that battered eastern Japan has left nine people dead, the public broadcaster NHK said on Sunday, after an “unprecedented” deluge that flooded more than a thousand homes and snarled up roads and rail services.
Torrential downpours that started late on Thursday have triggered landslide warnings and power outages, with forecasters issuing the highest-level heavy rain warning for the Chiba region for the first time.
A weather station in the prefecture recorded 300mm (nearly 12 inches) of rain in 24 hours, making it the area’s wettest August in six decades.
By Friday morning, the city of Chiba had logged more than three times the rainfall typically seen in the whole of August, Tokyo’s land ministry said.
Nine people have since died in the rains, NHK reported Sunday morning, citing its own tally.
Chiba’s disaster management office as of Saturday evening listed eight dead, some trapped inside submerged cars and others found on flooded streets.
More than 70 houses across the Chiba region were partially destroyed by the rain, the prefecture’s latest tally showed.
More than one thousand households reported being flooded, nearly 600 of which had water surge above the floorboards.
An estimated 1,200 cars also remain abandoned on roads, local media said, with authorities working on towing them away or using jacks to move them.
An official from Japan’s meteorological agency told a news conference on Thursday that it was “shaping up to be an unprecedented level of heavy rain”.
Scientists say human-driven climate change is making extreme weather more frequent, prolonged and intense.

title: At least five people dead in Indiana amid worst flooding in over 30 years, officials say
text:
At least five people are dead after devastating floods that swept through Indiana this week, officials said, as storms continued to batter the state on Saturday and first responders used boats to rescue more people from rising waters in neighborhoods along the White River in Indianapolis.
The mayor of Indianapolis, Joe Hogsett, and other state officials implored residents in areas at risk of flooding to heed any evacuation warnings at a news conference.
“Six inches of water can stall out any vehicle. Eight inches of water can move a vehicle off a road. And then three inches of water can actually take somebody off their feet too. Flooded water is very, very dangerous,” Jerry Martin, the deputy chief of the Indianapolis fire department, said at the briefing.
“The water is still rising. And it will be rising all day long,” Todd Wilson, director of the city’s public works department, said at the news conference.
Farther east in Delaware county, sheriff’s deputies on Friday found the body of a 58-year-old woman whom they believe died after trying to drive through floodwaters. They also recovered the body of a teenager who was first reported missing on Wednesday after jumping into a river. Earlier in the week, a four-year-old boy was killed after a tree fell on his home in Jennings county.
Flash flood warnings were issued for north-eastern Hendricks county and northern Marion county in central Indiana.
Authorities described the deluge’s effects as unlike anything seen in roughly 30 years.
The National Weather Service reported that more than 11in (28cm) of rain fell over a two-day period in some areas. The White River crested at more than 24ft (7.32 meters) in the communities of Anderson and Noblesville, surpassing records set in 1913.
The unprecedented nature of the flooding has stretched the capacity of first responders. Officials also said flooding had been observed in areas not historically affected.
Mike Braun, Indiana’s Republican governor, confirmed on Saturday that Donald Trump intended to approve his request for federal resources to help in response to the flooding and the recovery. Trump has approved a higher percentage of aid requests for Republican-led states than for Democratic-led states in his second term, according to research for the nonpartisan Urban Institute.
Authorities estimated that about 400 people evacuated parts of northern Indianapolis on their own, while the governor’s office reported more than 350 evacuations had occurred in Delaware county and that a senior mobile home community in Tipton county was being evacuated. Rescues and welfare checks also were happening in Fayette county.
Rita Reith, a spokesperson with the Indianapolis fire department, said 95 people and 45 pets had been rescued as of late afternoon. Dispatchers had received hundreds of calls for service throughout the day.
As of Saturday afternoon, more than 150,000 people were experiencing power outages, according to the northern Indiana public service company.

title: Hawaii braces for direct hit from Tropical Storm Lala
text:
Tropical Storm Lala is set to hit Hawaii’s Big Island with hurricane force in a matter of hours, bringing dangerous winds, heavy rainfall and high surf in a sign of what a strengthening “super” El Niño in the Pacific may bring.
The tropical storm is currently about 420 miles (675km) south-east of Hilo on the archipelago’s largest island, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa) said in its latest advisory, packing winds of 60mph (97km/h). Lala is forecast to strengthen into a hurricane as it approaches the Big Island.
Hurricane warnings have been issued for Hawaii county, which covers the Big Island, and a tropical storm warnings for the island of Maui, Molokai and Kahoolawe to its north-west.
Rainfall totals of 8-12in are predicted across Maui and the Big Island, with up to 25in in certain pockets. A storm surge of 1-3ft is also forecast as the storm comes ashore on Saturday.
Noaa’s Weather Prediction Center said Hawaii “faces life-threatening flash floods and mudslides as Tropical Storm Lala approaches”.
Hawaii’s governor, Josh Green, proclaimed a state of emergency.
“Tropical Storm Lala poses a serious threat to our state, particularly Hawaii Island – and we are taking action now to ensure resources are available where they are needed,” Green said.
“Our state and county emergency teams are coordinating closely with federal partners. I urge everyone to secure their homes, gather essential supplies, review their family emergency plans and follow updates from trusted official sources. Please take this storm seriously and look out for one another.”
Residents have been advised to clear gutters and drains and move valuables off the ground, seal gaps in doors and remove tree limbs that threaten their properties.
“Stay away from beaches and coastal areas where rough surf and rip currents could sweep you away,” Hawaii’s emergency management agency said.
On Friday, flood watches were in effect for the islands of Kauai, Niihau and Oahu from Saturday evening through Sunday night, and for the islands of Lanai, Molokai, Kahoolawe, Maui and Hawaii from Friday through Saturday night.
Hawaii was last hit by a “major” hurricane in 1992, when Hurricane Iniki caused at least six deaths and billions of dollars in damage.
If Lala’s center moves over the Big Island, it will be the first direct strike of a tropical cyclone for the island since Tropical Storm Darby in 2016. Two years earlier, the more powerful Tropical Storm Iselle caused widespread wind damage and power outages throughout the island, reported the Honolulu Star-Advertiser.
Hawaii county’s mayor, Kimo Alameda, said residents should brace for possible damaging winds, flooding rain, high surf, power outages, loss of communications and road closures.
“This is a quickly evolving situation and we urge our residents to act now to prepare for the storm by checking your emergency supplies, securing your property and contacting neighbors who may need assistance,” Alameda said in a news release.
“Readiness requires all of us, and with a storm this close, a slight change in its track can greatly enhance rain and wind hazards across the island. We encourage everyone to stay safe, stay connected, and be prepared to hunker down and stay home during severe weather.”
The Hawai‘i Volcanoes national park closed access to the summit of Mauna Loa, Earth’s largest active volcano, on Thursday afternoon, with plans to close the welcome center, all trails and the Nahuku lava tube. “It’s gonna be weird to see a giant hurricane be on top of that volcano erupting! Stay safe, everybody,” noted a visitor to the park’s Facebook page.
Lala’s approach comes as a powerful El Niño has formed in the central equatorial Pacific Ocean, with temperatures already so high that Noaa now predicts a 69% chance of a “historic event that would exceed the strength of previous El Niño events dating back to 1950” when it peaks between October and December.
El Niño, a natural climate pattern when sea surface temperatures in the central and eastern Pacific Ocean become unusually warm, tends to promote hurricane activity in the Pacific while suppressing it in the Atlantic.
Also in the Pacific, Tropical Storm Hernan formed on Thursday but was not threatening land and was weakening while moving south. Hernan was about 1,505 miles west-south-west of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula of Mexico with maximum sustained winds of about 40mph, the National Hurricane Center said.
In the Atlantic Ocean, former Tropical Storm Cristobal weakened and degenerated into a post-tropical remnant on Thursday, the center said. It was about 500 miles west of the Azores and did not threaten land.
The Associated Press contributed reporting

title: âUnprecedentedâ rain kills five in Japan as thousands stranded at airport
text:
At least five people have died in eastern Japan after “unprecedented” heavy rain that left nearly 7,000 stranded at Tokyo’s Narita airport and forced thousands to take refuge in government buildings.
The torrential rains hit Chiba prefecture, east of Tokyo, on Thursday night, triggering landslide warnings and power outages. Evacuation orders were issued for more than 400,000 people in Chiba and other areas, and about 45,000 homes lost power, as 115mm of rain fell hourly, approximately the same amount usually recorded for the whole month of August.
It was the first time the Japan Meteorological Agency has issued the highest level-5 warning for heavy rains and landslides for the prefecture.
The body of a man, believed to be in his 60s or 70s, was found floating in a flooded road in the city of Ichikawa, while a 66-year-old woman was killed when her car got trapped in flood waters in the city of Sakura. Two other people are reported to have died after being unable to escape from their cars during the flooding. Soldiers have been dispatched to the area to help with relief efforts.
“This case was an extremely unusual situation,” Chiba governor Toshihito Kumagai told reporters on Friday morning. “I have responded to many disasters in the past, but I have never experienced a case like this.”
Approximately 7,000 passengers spent the night at Narita, one of Tokyo’s main international airports, while 1,700 people sought shelter at the Chiba prefectural government building.
Footage from public broadcaster NHK showed water spurting violently from what appeared to be a maintenance hole and exceeding the height of a nearby five-storey building in Chiba’s central ward.
A woman in Ichikawa told NHK the rain “happened all of a sudden so it was a complete surprise”.
“The power is out so I’m worried whether I can open my business in the next couple of days,” she said.
A traveller from the UK who gave his name as Philip told AFP that he had to go through a nine-hour journey, including a taxi ride, before finally arriving at the airport early on Friday morning.
With a sleeping bag in hand, he said he has “just been trying to get some sleep and watching Netflix”.
“Just get on with it, really. Nothing else you can do,” he said.
Rain had eased by Friday but authorities are warning of the dangers of flooding in the area.
“For rivers where the risk of flooding is already high, please take action to protect your lives in any way possible,” said Kazuhito Shimamoto of the ministry of land, infrastructure, transport and tourism.
“There are also rivers where the risk of flooding is expected to increase further, so please check the evacuation advisories issued by your local municipalities and evacuate early.”
Meteorologists in Japan say that climate breakdown is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events.
Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed to this report

title: Little rain on the horizon as England and Wales experience driest July on record
text:
England has experienced its driest July since records began in 1836, receiving only 6.5mm of rainfall – 10% of the country’s long-term meteorological average for the month. Wales also experienced its driest-ever July, while Northern Ireland recorded its eighth driest. Scotland was the only country in the UK not to set new records but still received only 69% of its average rainfall for July compared with the long-term average. Southern England faced the worst of the dry conditions with some areas, including the Sussex coast, receiving less than 0.2mm of rain in July. This resulted in widespread low moisture content within the soil, enabling temperatures to reach the high 30s celsius.
Looking ahead, despite notable spells of rain in the north, parts of southern England may receive only the odd shower for the rest of August. Throughout the summer, forecast models have hinted at more unsettled weather reaching the south-east of England at a 10-day range. However, as time edged closer the rain was largely confined to north-western parts of Britain, failing to reach the south-east with any significance. With much uncertainty within forecast models, the risk of this dry period persisting is not out of the question.
There is a disturbance in the Atlantic, approximately 1,000 miles east of the Lesser Antilles. The National Hurricane Centre has predicted an 80% chance of the cyclone forming in the next 48 hours as a short-lived tropical depression. If such a system does strengthen, it will become the fourth named storm of the 2026 Atlantic hurricane season and would be named Dolly. Regardless of any development, there will be a risk of gusty winds and heavy rainfall in Lesser Antilles on Friday night and into Saturday. This year’s strong El Niño is expected to play a significant role in lessening hurricane activity within the Atlantic.
In India, the monsoon continues to cause devastation, particularly in eastern regions where flooding in Assam has caused 100 deaths as of 10 August. Flooding caused by rivers overflowing has resulted in 700,000 people being displaced over the last month. This includes 300,000 displaced near the Brahmaputra, one of the largest rivers in Asia. The monsoon also brought significant lightning, which resulted in the deaths of 14 people in eastern India on the 4 August, including 10 in the district of Giridih. Many of the dead were farm workers, caught in open agricultural fields where there is a lack of shelter to provide safety when such storms arrive.

title: How can we talk about this extreme weather now that itâs a battleground in the culture wars?
text:
In this fragmented but supposedly mild country, watching and talking about the weather forecast is meant to be a reassuring, unifying activity. Collectively, we have created and maintained a national climate narrative of small disappointments and pleasures. The first weather forecaster to appear on British TV, George Cowling, made his debut on the BBC in January 1954, predicting that “tomorrow would be rather windy”, but “a good day to hang out the washing”. For most of the 72 years since, such brief, carefully calibrated broadcasts have provided people from Aberdeen to Penzance with practical information, small talk and minor grumbles about essentially the same situation: living in a country where the weather is constantly changing, in a paradoxically unchanging way.
Yet like the traditional British climate, that common weather culture may now be evaporating. “Met Office considers issuing red ‘extreme heat warning’ across Britain while nation enjoys ‘incredible summer’,” said the headline above the forecast on the GB News website on Monday, caught between terror and delight at the latest heatwave. As the climate crisis has affected this country in more and more unmistakable but uneven ways, TV weather forecasters have increasingly struggled to find the right language to describe this transformation’s daily consequences. Their struggle influences and exemplifies that of many Britons to understand, and work out what we think about, the apparent end of the weather patterns we expected to shape our whole lives.
Across all the British TV broadcasters, sometimes within the same bulletin, or even the same sentence, weather forecasters now present sunshine as welcome and oppressive; high temperatures as miraculous and unbearable; rain as an inconvenience and desperately needed; cloud cover as depressing and a relief. Tanned forecasters in sundresses, emphasising the positives for domestic holidaymakers of another record-breaking summer, alternate with grim-faced forecasters suggesting we are experiencing a weather apocalypse.
Meanwhile, the wildly differing effects of the climate crisis on different areas, and from one season to another, are further fracturing Britain’s weather conversation into a babble of separate, sometimes conflicting discourses. This year, parts of the country have experienced such contrasting summers – wetter than usual in western Scotland, desert-like in southern England – that we can no longer say they share broadly the same northern European climate, as had been assumed for centuries. In an era of separatism and nationalism, another major binding element of the UK may be falling away.
Beneath the relatively placid surface of our previous weather culture, there were always some tensions and contradictions. In a 2025 academic paper, British Heatwave Discourse (1985–2023): from Ice Cream to Armageddon?, Thijs van Dooremalen and Philip Smith analysed articles about heatwaves in the national press. They found that until 2000 positive and negative coverage coexisted in roughly equal quantities, “often in the same newspaper”. From 2000 to 2014, the balance shifted slowly towards the negative, as the climate crisis became a mainstream worry. Yet only from 2015 did an “Apocalyptic genre” of heatwave articles begin to become dominant; and a “Romantic genre” of celebratory coverage remains. In a country where many people still spend much of the year feeling cold, the idea of hot weather as a liberation is likely to linger, for some, for decades to come.
For other Britons, heatwaves have become political flashpoints, their causes to be furiously contested, their existence even denied. During the record heat of 2022, “weather forecasters faced unprecedented levels of trolling”, the BBC reported, including “hundreds of abusive tweets or emails questioning their reports and telling them to ‘get a grip’… ‘it’s just summer’”. Some of these climate crisis deniers described advice on how to stay cool as “pandering to the ‘woke brigade’”, and accused the BBC and Met Office of “scaremongering” to help the then Conservative government impose unneeded green policies.
This summer, some of these conspiratorial arguments have re-emerged. But with the Tories having in effect turned against net zero, joined by Reform UK, Restore Britain and most of the rightwing media, disagreeing with weather forecasters who express alarm about our changing climate has become more mainstream. Discussing the weather is no longer just small talk, but also a battlefield in the culture wars.
No wonder forecasters often sound unsure or extremely cautious about what tone to adopt on air. In 2023, the BBC’s Tomasz Schafernaker gave a very careful interview to the Big Issue. “While our language remains largely the same,” he said, “we have adapted it to include references to climate change. We must be mindful that prolonged periods of sun and heat are not always good news … However, there are often areas in the UK where the weather is much more comfortable, [so] highlighting that it’s not ‘all bad’ is important. It’s a balance that we assess on a daily basis.”
Yet three years on, his broadcasts have become less neutral. “The savage summer continues across Europe,” he said on the BBC weather website last Thursday afternoon. “It’s been excruciatingly hot …” On BBC One last Sunday evening, while giving this week’s UK forecast, he kept making gestures of helplessness and disbelief. It was like a weather bulletin from a dystopian drama.
Such interventions no longer seem melodramatic. “The climate of the 20th century has now gone,” says Mike Kendon, a Met Office scientist and co-author of State of the UK Climate in 2025, published last month. So far, this year’s weather has been more extreme. Even more than the heat, summer drought and winter floods, its key feature has been the weather getting stuck in one state for months – a characteristic of harsh continental climates, rather than the changeable one around which our society has been built. So it’s possible that next summer will feature relentless rain, not drought, and that other seasons will continue to stall as well, damaging the economy, everyday life and public health.
Britons are world famous for their weather stoicism. But this stoicism has been created by centuries of relatively minor weather discomforts and disasters. How the forecasters, and the rest of us, will react as the climate crisis intensifies – in our private behaviours and assumptions as well as our public lives – is a question we are only in the early stages of answering.
- 
  Andy Beckett is a Guardian columnist

title: Severe storms cut power supply to 540,000 homes in US midwest
text:
Power supply was cut on Thursday to about 540,000 homes and businesses across the US midwest as severe storms battered the region, data from PowerOutage.us showed.
Indiana was the hardest-hit state, with more than 267,000 outages, representing about 8% of its roughly 3.3 million customers, the data showed.
“Rounds of severe thunderstorms will threaten the plains, midwest and east into Thursday with damaging wind gusts, while repeated downpours could trigger dangerous flash flooding,” the weather forecaster AccuWeather said in a statement.
First responders had rescued many people from floodwaters on Wednesday as utility crews cleared trees and wires downed by the severe storms in the midwest that have unleashed tornadoes, heavy rains and flash flooding across the region for several days.
A four-year-old boy was killed when a tree fell on a home in Geneva, Indiana, during Tuesday’s storms, the Jennings county sheriff’s office said. Ohio’s governor, Mike DeWine, said a resident of Roseville died during a health emergency when first responders, faced with flooded roads, couldn’t reach them.
Officials in Portage, Indiana, were investigating whether the severe weather played a role in a reported house explosion that killed a person.
Indiana’s hardest-hit utility was Northern Indiana Public Service Company, taking out services to about 258,885 homes and businesses, or about 55% of its roughly 468,000 customers in the state. Nipsco is a unit of Indiana energy firm NiSource.
In a statement, the utility said it was assessing damage and would provide estimated restoration times when the task was complete, but warned that restoration could take days in some areas as the damage was extensive.
“There is widespread damage to electric infrastructure, including downed poles, power lines and trees,” it added.
Duke Energy said it was pulling in 1,000 workers to restore power to more than 171,000 customers across greater Cincinnati in Ohio over the past 24 hours.
“They’ll work alongside our employees and contractors in Ohio and Kentucky to safely restore service for our customers as quickly as possible,” Andy Cassidy, Duke Energy’s storm director, said in a statement.
About 46,200 homes and businesses were without power, or about 6% of its roughly 768,281 customers in Ohio.
Authorities in Ohio and western Pennsylvania have reported numerous water rescues. DeWine sent 40 Ohio army national guard members to help in two counties east of Columbus, and he said dozens of local departments also responded to help, including from West Virginia.
Reuters and the Associated Press contributed reporting

title: âEveryone is scaredâ: flood-hit Porto Alegre braces for another El NiÃ±o
text:
In the backstreets of Porto Alegre, a state capital in southern Brazil, you can still see signs of the devastating flood that swept through the city two years ago: scattered debris, waterlogged homes and destroyed businesses.
In May 2024, flooding killed 183 people in the state of Rio Grande do Sul and displaced more than 600,000. The neighbourhood of Sarandi was one of the hardest-hit parts of Porto Alegre, with water levels reaching up to 5 metres above normal, completely submerging many of its streets.
“Most people are still suffering the mental health consequences of the flood,” says Luís Rogério “Jamaika” Machado, a community leader in Sarandi.
“They lost absolutely everything. Unable to rebuild their houses, most have become deeply depressed.”
In June, meteorologists announced the imminent return of El Niño, the naturally occurring phenomenon caused by rising sea-surface temperatures in the equatorial Pacific but the effects of which are greatly aggravated by the climate crisis. El Niño, which disrupts weather patterns across the globe, is likely to cause extreme rainfall and flooding in southern Brazil.
Jamaika lives in an urban quilombo, a Brazilian settlement founded by escaped enslaved people or their descendants. Quilombo dos Machado is one of 11 such territories in Porto Alegre and served as a centre of solidarity for the entire Sarandi area during the flood, distributing food, clothing and medical assistance to thousands of families.
Now Porto Alegre’s flood-hit communities, though still recovering from one of Brazil’s deadliest climate disasters, face renewed threats from this year’s developing El Niño as incomplete flood defences and government relocation schemes fuel fears of displacement and deepen a climate justice crisis.
Sarandi, along with other poorer areas of the city, is one such example. Despite being among those who are the least responsible for the emissions that cause climate breakdown, people there experienced the worst effects of the 2024 flood.
This imbalance has led the Porto Alegre research group at the Metropolis Observatory, part of Brazil’s National Institutes of Science and Technology (INCT), to call the flood a climate justice crisis.
Now, these same people are bracing for yet another climate-induced disaster.
The first storms caused by the latest El Niño arrived in Rio Grande do Sul in June, with rain and strong winds disrupting the region. Rising river levels affected at least 200 municipalities, leaving 1,800 people homeless and many more outraged by the government’s inaction over the past two years.
“El Niño peaks in December, January and February,” says Wilfran Moufouma-Okia, chief of climate prediction at World Meteorological Organization. “So we are just at the beginning.”
For people in Porto Alegre, the headlines bring renewed fears.
“Our house was completely submerged. We lost everything,” says Suelen Telles, a pre-school teacher who lives in Sarandi. “We’ve since returned to our house, and we’re terrified of losing everything again. Everyone on our street is scared.”
After losing her house in 2024, Solange Rodrigues Correa moved in with her grandson in Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros, an archipelago on the margins of the city. News reports have caused her to worry about the flood waters returning, and Correa, who suffered a stroke due to the stress of the 2024 floods, has not slept for several nights in a row.
“Once again, what will become of us?” she says.
Rudimar Dal Asta, a priest in Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros and one of the community leaders who helped in rescue missions during the previous flood, says the government has given assurances that there is an evacuation plan, but they have not seen it yet. “Our escape route is to run to the bridge, just like we did in 2024,” he says.
Over the past few months, Porto Alegre has repaired floodgates, replaced sewer covers, and rebuilt a section of the Sarandi dyke. Mayor Sebastião Melo announced that improvements to pumping stations – which were shut off in 2024 due to the risk of electric shock – would be completed by November.
“We’ve finished many projects,” says Melo. “Others are now under construction, and others have yet to be started. Porto Alegre is now a much more protected city.”
In the south of the city, however, the preparations remain makeshift: sandbags, movable barriers and floating pumps. Certain neighbourhoods, such as Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros, do not have adequate protective infrastructure and people are apprehensive.
“The flood protection systems are still incomplete,” says Leonardo Bauer Maggi of the Movement of People Affected by Dams (MAB), a large grassroots social movement that supports the affected population.
“They installed emergency sirens, but we don’t know where to run if they sound,” he says. “No shelters have been prepared.”
The Porto Alegre administration is now being sued for the failures of the flood protection system in 2024. Last year, the state court of auditors revealed that a lack of investment and a series of other failures combined to weaken flood-protection measures in Porto Alegre.
Auditors held Melo, as well as the former mayor Nelson Marchezan Júnior, responsible for a “serious disregard for the duty of care”. The public prosecutors’ office has since sued the city of Porto Alegre for 50m reais (£7.3m) to reimburse 19 neighbourhoods affected by the flood.
“We want to prepare for El Niño, but we still don’t know how,” says Jamaika. “When the water rises, the only alternative presented by the government is to leave the area in an emergency.”
Last month, the state government launched Prepara RS, an emergency initiative to assist policymakers, organise volunteers and provide public guidance about imminent storms to the people of Rio Grande do Sul. The initiative has transferred 32.3m reais to 138 municipalities across the state.
In a statement praising the quality of its monitoring systems and its flood defences, the state government said: “In recent years, the government has been making progress in a series of structural, operational and strategic improvements to prepare the state to face extreme events, including possible negative effects of El Niño.”
Yet the state government acknowledged that it had failed to predict the recent rise of river levels, which have now flooded cities across the region.
A recent study by the Celso Furtado International Centre for Development Policy and the Climate and Society Institute revealed that the state government had spent less than 0.5% of its climate budget on mitigating future disasters.
Maggi says the people most affected by the floods are working class, who had to borrow money to rebuild their homes. “The water receded, but the flood didn’t pass,” he says.
About two-thirds of people affected in Rio Grande do Sul had a family income at or below 5,000 reais (£730) a month, according to the Brazilian Institute of Geography and Statistics.
Jamaika says nearly 7,000 families in his quilombo were affected by the flood – and 4,500 of them have not yet recovered, which he blames on a lack of government assistance.
In 2024, the federal government distributed 5,100 reais of “reconstruction aid” to about 430,000 affected families, totalling 2.2bn reais, based on government data. But Jamaika says this aid was woefully inadequate for those in his community. “Rebuilding their lives becomes almost impossible. What house can you rebuild with 5,000 reais?”
Many in Porto Alegre accuse the city and state governments of using floods to displace them. Betânia Alfonsin, a law professor and member of the Metropolis Observatory, says houses in flood-risk areas are demolished when people relocate and are often refurbished for wealthier owners who can afford risk mitigation.
The classification of “risk area” is often used selectively, says Alfonsin. “It’s a stamp of expulsion for the poor.”
Most people in these areas are relocated through government programmes such as My Home, My Life, which offers financing for new homes. However, people say the mortgage is burdensome. “They push My Home, My Life as a solution, which we call ‘My Debt’,” jokes Solange Correa. “You had a house – now you get a debt for life.”
Another federal government housing programme, Assisted Purchase, gives 200,000 reais towards a new property. In Porto Alegre, 9,477 people applied, with 5,800 of those approved. After receiving funds, the old homes are demolished, leaving people remaining in rubble in neighbourhoods such as Ilha Grande dos Marinheiros and Sarandi, which resemble war zones.
“This programme is problematic because it negotiates family by family rather than community,” says Alfonsin, who argues that it promotes the dispersal and destruction of communities.
More than 50% of Assisted Purchase recipients bought homes in other cities. For Jamaika, the programme “is yet another expression of gentrification”.

title: Powerful storms in US midwest leave three dead and 800,000 without power
text:
Powerful storms swept across the midwest on Tuesday, leaving three dead and more than 800,000 without power in four states as winds gusts of more than 80mph (130km/h) tore down trees and power lines.
In Indiana, a four-year-old child died after a tree fell on his home in Geneva Township and a person died in a suspected weather-related house explosion in Portage, a city about 30 miles south-east of Chicago.
Mike DeWine, Ohio’s governor, said one person died after flooding obstructed first responders from reaching the individual in Roseville. DeWine urged Ohioans to prepare for more dangerous storms as the National Weather Service warned of flash flooding, tornadoes and dangerous straight-line winds.
“I encourage everyone to pay close attention to local media reports and take these weather warnings seriously,” he said. “Even after the storms exit the state, flooding will remain a serious concern.”
The National Weather Service’s storm prediction center said it had recorded straight-line winds, known as derecho, at speeds of 99mph in Gary, Indiana.
DeWine also signed a proclamation declaring a state of emergency in Perry and Muskingum counties. Severe flooding caused residents to be evacuated by swift water rescue teams.
“Even after the storms exit the state, flooding will remain a serious concern,” the governor said. The National Weather Service warned of “considerable flooding” in Ohio through Friday.
Nearly 800,000 electricity customers across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio and Kentucky were still without power as of Wednesday morning, poweroutage.us reported.
Utility provider AEP said the area of Columbus, Ohio, experienced gusts of more than 80mph and trees falling on power lines. It said it had more than 2,000 workers trying to restore electricity.
Downed trees and power lines from the storms that hit Portage, Indiana, prevented emergency crews from accessing the house fire where a person died.
Many trees were blocking roads, prompting several officers to park a mile away and run toward the home to try to respond. “It seemed that every road had a tree down,” said Mike Candiano, the Portage police chief.
Rob Maynard, Portage’s police captain, said at a news conference, reported by NBC News, that the storms “probably the most severe weather event that any of us here can remember”.
The child died when a tree fell on his bedroom about 3.30pm in Jennings county. Cody Low, the county chief sheriff’s deputy, said: “Contributions are probably wind and the storms that came through this county earlier.”
Elsewhere, 16 people at a prison in Grafton, Ohio, were taken to hospitals after lightning struck as inmates returned from an evening meal. There were two confirmed tornadoes near Chicago, the National Weather Service said.
In Columbus, Mayor Andrew Ginther said at a news conference that power could be out for days.
“I want to encourage everybody to plan on a very different next couple of days and rest of the week,” Ginther said. “Things are not going to be fully restored and back to normal later today or tomorrow, the day after that.”
In a post on X, Ginther said: “Neighbors, we’re all in this storm recovery together. Our departments are answering the call, taking care of each other and helping to keep everyone safe.”

title: Mass evacuations in Beijing as Typhoon Dolphin brings more torrential rain to China
text:
Thousands of people have been evacuated from areas at risk of flooding and landslides in Beijing, as the remnants of Typhoon Dolphin continue to bring torrential rain to northern and central China.
Forecasters warned on Tuesday that the Chinese capital could receive more than 150mm of rain over the following 24 hours, with some districts forecast to exceed 200mm – more than one-third of Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm.
Beijing remained under an orange rainstorm warning, the second-highest level, on Wednesday, with the heaviest rainfall expected across the morning.
Authorities closed hundreds of tourist attractions and campsites on Wednesday, with more than 1,300 tourists evacuated or turned away. Meanwhile, over 5,000 elderly people were moved from care facilities and about 1,800 people living around construction projects in mountainous or riverside areas were relocated.
The rain also disrupted Wednesday morning’s commute. Official local media reported that 250 bus routes had been suspended and trains were running at reduced speeds on 10 metro lines.
Dolphin, the strongest typhoon to hit China so far this year, has weakened after making landfall in the eastern province of Zhejiang on Sunday, but its remnants have continued to draw large amounts of tropical moisture deep inland and drench central and northern parts of the country.
The neighbouring Hebei province was also on alert for mountain floods, landslides and other geological hazards. Authorities said they had dispatched 623 teams to mountainous areas and equipped more than 2,100 at-risk villages with satellite phones or satellite messaging terminals to maintain communications during emergencies, according to state media.
In the central province of Henan, authorities raised the warning for torrential rain to the highest-level red alert on Wednesday morning, as downpours continue to batter large swathes of the province. More heavy rain was forecast through Thursday morning, with 24-hour rainfall totals of up to 350mm expected in some areas.
Classes, business operations and non-essential outdoor activities have been suspended in the affected areas of Henan. Residents were told to avoid deep flood waters and evacuate immediately if vehicles stall in water, state media reports.
China, the world’s second-largest economy, is increasingly exposed to destructive weather events that scientists link to climate change. This year is proving particularly tough due to the emergence of the El Niño weather pattern that is driving up temperatures and fuelling more frequent and intense typhoons.
Rainfall records have also been broken elsewhere in central China. Wugang in Henan received 209.5mm in a day and Xiangyang in neighbouring Hubei recorded 169.1mm, both the highest single-day rainfall totals for August, according to state media.
Reuters contributed to this report

title: Typhoon Dolphin hits Beijing as city braces for one-third of annual rainfall over 24 hours
text:
Typhoon Dolphin hit China’s capital on Tuesday as the storm caused flooding in parts of Beijing’s Shunyi district. Rains are forecast to intensify overnight.
Although the storm has been downgraded to a tropical depression, several districts in Beijing activated the highest level of emergency flood responses as the city braced for one-third of its annual rainfall, which is expected over the next 24 hours.
The ministry of water resources activated a level 4 emergency response and dispatched personnel to badly hit areas in Beijing and the neighbouring port city of Tianjin.
Chinese state media reported that Beijing ordered more than 250 flood-control teams to be on standby and to prepare flood barriers at subway stations, hospitals and elderly care facilities.
From Tuesday evening through to Thursday, most areas in Beijing will experience heavy downpours with a cumulative rainfall of more than 150mm in 24 hours, the city’s meteorological service has forecast. That compares with Beijing’s average annual rainfall of 528mm, the bulk of which normally falls between June and September.
Four districts on Beijing’s outskirts activated level 1 emergency flood responses. In the mountainous district of Mentougou in western Beijing, authorities issued the highest level of flood emergency alert on Tuesday and advised people to stay indoors and avoid travelling to mountainous areas and rivers.
The strongest typhoon to hit China this year, Dolphin has proved an unusually resilient storm system, travelling nearly 6,000km (3,728 miles) before making landfall over the weekend, drenching China’s eastern coast and bringing with it a sprawling cloud field.
More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China over the weekend, amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.
Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved.
In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening.
Early on Tuesday Dolphin moved over the central Chinese province of Hubei, a major auto and hi-tech electronics manufacturing hub and home to more than 58 million people.
On Tuesday, the national meteorological centre renewed an orange alert for heavy rain, the second-highest warning level, with north-western Hubei expected to receive up to 250mm in a 24-hour period. Hubei authorities have issued a yellow warning for cities including Xiangyang, Huanggang and Suizhou, citing a heightened risk of flooding and landslides.
Scenic areas across the province have announced temporary closures, including the popular Three Gorges Dam tourist area in Yichang. Of 107 major highway and waterway construction projects under way in the province, 26 projects deemed high-risk have been suspended.
In neighbouring Henan province, authorities issued a flash-flood alert as the storm continues to channel moisture northward.
Japan is also preparing for landslides, flooding and strong winds after the Japan Meteorological Agency said Typhoon Chan-hom could move across Japan’s mainland later on Tuesday.
Reuters contributed to this report

title: Typhoon Dolphin: more than a million people evacuated in China as record rainfall dumped on Shanghai
text:
More than a million people were moved to safety across eastern China by Sunday evening as powerful Typhoon Dolphin made landfall amid fears torrential rain would cause flooding and landslides.
Wenzhou, a coastal city in Zhejiang province, said it relocated more than 900,000 people and opened more than 1,500 emergency shelters. In neighbouring Fujian, 98,900 people were moved from high-risk areas.
In Shanghai, 215,600 people were moved from areas considered at risk by Sunday evening, substantially higher than an earlier figure of 30,300.
A weather station in central Shanghai recorded nearly 313mm of rain in the 24 hours to 7am on Monday, its highest 24-hour rainfall in more than 150 years of records. Another station in the city recorded nearly 400mm. The hashtag “Shanghai turns into the sea” began trending on the Chinese social media platform Weibo, as videos circulated showing streets flooded around the Wukang Mansion, one of the city’s best-known tourist landmarks.
The average rainfall recorded across Zhejiang from Friday evening to Monday morning reached 173mm, reportedly surpassing the levels seen during previous major typhoons including Lekima and Bavi.
Dolphin weakened rapidly to a tropical storm by 5am on Monday. But as the storm continued to move northwards and farther inland, heavy rain was forecast across large parts of eastern and central China, extending north into Shandong and affecting Henan, Hubei, Anhui, Jiangsu, Zhejiang and Shanghai.
Authorities maintained an orange alert for heavy rain and warned that days of intense rain could trigger widespread flooding and landslides through Wednesday, urging people to stay indoors during the heavy downpours. Forecasters in China predicted some areas could see 200-400mm (7.9–15.7 inches) of rainfall over the coming days.
The storm forced Shanghai’s two airports to cancel more than 1,300 flights. Public transport services, including many local trains, have been suspended in the financial hub.
Zhejiang’s Ningbo international airport, about 150km south of Shanghai, will resume flight operations from midday (0400 GMT) on Monday. But the airport warned some journeys may yet be delayed or cancelled.
Provincial capital Hangzhou resumed subway services on Monday morning, after halting some train operations on Sunday.
Elsewhere, Dolphin fuelled intense heat over Hong Kong on Sunday, pushing the city to its highest ever temperature of 36.9C. The extremely hot weather was expected to continue into Tuesday, officials said.
In Taiwan, ferry services were suspended and more than 180 flights were cancelled as the storm brought downpours and strong winds on Sunday.
Dolphin earlier swept through Japan’s southern Okinawa prefecture, injuring six people and cutting power to more than 50,000 buildings.
In the Philippines, the typhoon did not make landfall in the country’s north but intensified the seasonal monsoon rains, which flooded many areas of the main northern Luzon region, including around Manila.
Scientists say global warming has made extreme weather more likely, including more powerful typhoons.
