title: âWe canât make it better againâ: what Europeâs wildfires tell us about the climate crisis
text:
When Stefan Rahmstorf walked through the ruined streets of Dresden after the river Elbe flooded in 2002, and again when severe heat killed 70,000 people in Europe the following summer, the German climatologist wondered if worsening weather would make the political world “wake up and do something really decisively” to cut emissions.
But two decades and 750bn tons of atmospheric carbon pollution later, Rahmstorf is still wondering when the wake-up call will come. Last week, as he was surfing off France’s Atlantic coast with his partner, he watched towering smoke plumes darken the sky as a ferocious inferno raged outside Bordeaux.
“The sun through the smoke was looking really blood red, and it put the whole landscape into an eerie orange-coloured tint, like being on Mars or in some dystopian sci-fi movie,” says Rahmstorf. “It felt totally surreal.”
Europe is suffering through a hellish summer of relentless heat. I’m writing this from Berlin, where temperatures are set to reach 37C (99F) on Thursday – and ferocious wildfires that have broken records in France and Spain.
What are the impacts of this, and should it really have come as a surprise? All that and more, after the headlines.
Essential reads
- 
  ‘We have lost everything’: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons
- 
  ‘Race against time’: Japan earthquake death toll rises as rescue teams search for missing
- 
  Uganda begins emergency food handouts after 19 die from hunger
In focus
Rahmstorf had avoided summer holidays in the Mediterranean for years because of his knowledge of the science of climate breakdown, but he did not expect Europe’s cooler Atlantic coast to also be so hot. Yet as he looked back to the land from his surfboard on Wednesday last week, he saw a plume of smoke rising behind the dunes. Two days later, the fire that had caused it it had escalated into a blaze so great it generated a rare thunderstorm cloud capable of igniting even more fires. Rahmstorf cut his holiday in Lacanau a day short and headed to smoke-choked Bordeaux on Friday evening, eager to take the train back to Germany the next day.
“The air was much better when we woke up Saturday morning,” he says. “But the idea of having to inhale this kind of air for any length of time seemed something we really wanted to avoid.”
This summer’s fire weather across the EU has broken records for severity for this time of year, data published on Thursday shows, while more of France has already burned than in any previous full year on record. More than 300,000 people across France and Spain were forced to flee homes and tourist accommodation within a week, and some are returning to burned-out homes and destroyed belongings.
The ever-increasing toll of heat and fire has risen almost too fast for scientists to track. Rapid analyses have found June’s heatwave would have been “virtually impossible” in a world without climate breakdown, while the recent level of soil dryness in western Europe – a driver of bigger blazes – was made five times more likely. Heatwaves are estimated to have claimed at least 10,000 lives and cost grain farmers €2bn in lost crops.
Climate scientists say the extreme weather ravaging the world is in line with what models have long predicted, though some disasters appear to be striking earlier and with more strength than expected. The underlying relationship between fossil fuel pollution and global temperatures was well known even to oil companies, who were at the forefront of corporate efforts to stymie action to cut pollution, as far back as the 1970s. A study Rahmstorf co-authored in 2023 found ExxonMobil’s predictions of global heating over the following decades to have been mostly accurate, as skilful as independent academic and government models, and also very much at odds with its public statements on the matter.
“When you’re among young people, it’s hard for them to understand how long we’ve known all the basic facts about climate change,” said Rahmstorf, a scientist at the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research who has worked on the topic for 35 years. “Even when I started as a PhD student in the 1980s, it was very clear that our emissions were causing global warming and all the consequences it would have.”
Europe has warmed about twice as fast as the global average and extreme weather events were already being strengthened by climate change when Rahmstorf was an early-career researcher. But it is only in the last brutal few years that the explosive effects of climate breakdown have been widely acknowledged as an immediate threat to the continent. A string of particularly deadly floods whose rains were made worse by carbon pollution – including Germany’s Ahrtal in 2021 and Spain’s Valencia in 2024 – have hit amid successive scorching summers that bring intense wildfires.
Yet even as Europe’s leaders acknowledge the scale and cause of the problem, they have weakened the very rules in place to stop it from getting worse. Two weeks ago, the European Commission proposed watering down the continent’s emissions trading system, a form of carbon market widely hailed as its most successful tool to cut pollution.
“What people are not getting is that we can’t turn this back – the CO2 to a large part remains in the air for thousands of years,” said Rahmstorf. “Some people think we can wait and, when it gets too bad, then we reduce emissions and things will get better again. People don’t realise that we can’t make it get better again. We can only prevent it from getting much worse.”

title: A âdecade on the Iberian âfrontlineâ has shown me that Europeâs âclimate âemergencyâ is âimpossible to âdeny
text:
Spain has changed immeasurably since I arrived here 10 years ago to begin work as the Guardian’s Madrid correspondent.
Over that time, the push for Catalan independence has exploded, sputtered and faded out; the Covid pandemic has hit with unimaginable ferocity, before seeming to linger for a face-masked eternity; and Podemos and Ciudadanos – the two upstart parties that once seemed likely to alter the Spanish political landscape irrevocably – have risen and fallen.
But one change has been so insistent, so undeniable and so painfully visible, that it has come to eclipse all others. A decade ago, perhaps naively, I could never have imagined how much time I would spend reporting the effects of the climate emergency here and in Portugal. Nor would I ever have imagined that things would get this bad, this fast.
The facts, however, speak for themselves. Europe is the fastest-heating continent, warming at a speed more than twice that of the global average, and the Iberian peninsula has become the sometimes scorched, sometimes sodden, frontline of the climate crisis. The wildfires still burning here and in France – which have led to the evacuation or confinement of approximately 330,000 people since last week – are merely the latest manifestation of all that.
It’s hard to think of a better example of all this than the autumn of 2024. At the end of September that year, the photographer Gonçalo Fonseca and I trudged around the northern Portuguese municipality of Albergaria-a-Velha, trekking through a landscape of blackened trees, burnt-out cars and ruined, roofless houses.
The fires that had inflicted the damage the previous week killed nine people, injured dozens more and razed 100,000 hectares of land across northern and central Portugal. They had been fuelled by strong winds, dry conditions and unseasonably hot temperatures of more than 30C (85F). It all inevitably brought back memories of the calamitous blazes of 2017, which claimed 66 lives.
João Oliveira, the head of the civil protection agency in Albergaria-a-Velha, showed me a picture on his mobile phone of a towering tidal wave of grey smoke preparing to engulf the town.
An annual fixture
He said there was no comparison whatsoever with the fires of previous years, adding: “The amount of energy the fire created, the amount of damage it did and the intensity and violence of the fire, were something we’d never seen before.”
Four weeks later, I parked my car on the edge of the eastern Spanish town of Utiel, pulled on my wellingtons and headed to see the aftermath of the deadly floods that had hit the Valencia region 48 hours earlier, killing more than 230 people. Ruined houses, wrecked cars, people speechless on the streets, and an inches-deep carpet of thick, sticky mud everywhere.
The only reference points I had for what I saw there and in the town of Chiva were the super El Niño I witnessed in northern Peru in 1998, and the devastation I reported on a month after the Nepal earthquake in April 2015. But these days, the kind of danger and destruction I thought I’d never see in Europe is becoming an almost annual fixture on the peninsula – and beyond.
Helena Smith, the Guardian’s correspondent in Greece, points out that warnings have long sounded from her part of the continent. “I still vividly recall Eleni Myrivili – who is now the UN’s global chief heat officer and was then newly installed as Athens’ heat maestro – saying, ‘Heat will be the story of the next decade,’” she said.
“That was in 2021. The same week I had written of apocalyptic scenes on the fringes of the Greek capital and ‘infernos redolent of Dante’s hell incinerating everything in their path’. It was inconceivable it could be worse. And, yet, every year it is: testimony to the irrefutable fact that the climate emergency is our runaway train, that temperatures in Athens are set to be on a par with Bahrain; that Spain and France are the new Greece, and London the Athens I first knew, in terms of heat, in the late 90s.”
Likewise, Angelique Chrisafis, the Guardian’s Paris correspondent, told me that much of her reporting has been focused on the impact of the climate crisis – including its attendant inequalities – since May’s record-breaking heatwave.
“I remember Issam, a 10-year-old boy in the southern suburbs of Paris whose top-floor school classroom reached 40C and whose badly insulated flat was hit by blazing sun against the windows all day, often leaving his mother dizzy and struggling to breathe,” she said.
Three weeks ago, I spoke to Jeanne Henny, a British woman who would have burned to death in her car had she not risked a three-point turn on a narrow cliff road as she fled the flames in Almería earlier this month.
And on Saturday afternoon I visited people who had been evacuated from their homes west of Madrid to a municipal sports centre on the outskirts of the capital. “[The sky] turned orange and looked very apocalyptic,” one man told me. “It felt like the end of the world.”
But of all the many climate emergency stories I’ve reported over the past few years, there are two that I still think about often.
In Utiel, I met Miguel Aleixandre, a young man who told me about the night of the floods in Valencia.
As the waters rose to a height of three metres, Miguel looked out across his dark neighbourhood and saw elderly neighbours signalling with candles at their windows. They were hoping to attract the attention of the rescuers who would, in some cases, arrive too late. Then he heard the sound of windows breaking and realised that the flood waters were pouring into the houses of people who would soon drown, trapped in their homes.
Fifteen months earlier, I had stood in a petrol station in the north-western Spanish town of Tábara listening to an account of the brave but fateful decision that had cost Ángel Martín his life the previous summer.
Desperate to prevent the wildfires in the Sierra de la Culebra from devouring his town, the 53-year-old builder’s yard owner climbed into his excavator to try to dig a firebreak. Within minutes, Martín and the vehicle were swallowed by the flames and the thick, black smoke. Video showing him emerging from the inferno, his clothes consumed by the flames, went around the world.
For a week or two at least, the figure of the burning, running, stumbling man became a symbol of the human consequences of the climate emergency. Martín suffered burns to 80% of his body and died in hospital three months later.
“We still talk about him a lot,” Martín’s friend, Montse Fernández Blanco, told me. “And I remember his jokes and what a good, happy person he was. The thing is he would have done it again because that’s what he was like.”
And yet, four years after Ángel Martín ran out of the flames, and two years after people died under the flood waters in Utiel, the same arguments, denial and political point-scoring continue to hamper efforts to prepare for the decades to come – decades that are all but certain to make all this seem mild.
We can hardly say we weren’t warned.

title: âWe have lost everythingâ: extreme rainfall across Asia brings flash floods and typhoons
text:
“It rained for 10 days and 10 nights, non-stop – I’d never seen anything like it,” says Anar Gul, a construction worker who lives in the remote district of Dur Baba in eastern Afghanistan.
The houses in his village are built from stone and mud, which makes them extremely vulnerable to heavy rains. After days of rain, Gul’s kitchen collapsed and his neighbour, Sayed Afsar Sadat, saw a large part of his house completely destroyed. “Rains like this are coming heavier and earlier each year,” says Sadat. “They are destroying the roads and washing away our crops. It’s impacting us directly.”
Last week, torrential rains and flash floods wiped out villages and towns in Afghanistan, leaving at least 31 people dead and hundreds missing. It’s been a similar picture in neighbouring countries, with the monsoon rains sparking chaos across the region. India, Bangladesh and Pakistan have all seen erratic, sudden heavy dumps of water.
Jesmin Akter lived in the city of Chattogram, on the south-eastern coast of Bangladesh, which received a record 412.3mm of rainfall in 24 hours in early July, leading to the flash flood that swept through the Banshkhali district where they live. She says her children “understand that we are in a very bad situation”.
Overnight the rains took the little they had; their poultry died, their paddy field flooded, their house collapsed and all their belongings in it – children’s books, school bags, toys, clothes, kitchen items – ruined.
Akter carried her six children through chest-deep water to her mother’s house. There they stayed in the crowded conditions for over a week until the water receded.
“We have lost everything,” Akter said. Their house beside the canal was not in a good condition, but a few months ago the family had repaired it. “Now the flood has destroyed it again. We have no money. We are surviving on the food assistance we receive from different organisations.” They have gone back to the ruins of their home, but her children sleep on plastic sheets laid on the wet floor and she worries for their safety, especially that the unsanitary conditions will lead to disease. Her daughter has developed a fever.
As wildfires rage across Europe and North America, the unprecedented rains continue elsewhere. While South Korea swings between heatwave and downpour, in Japan and Vietnam torrential rain has led to landslides. China, meanwhile, has seen bouts of extreme rainfall since the flood season began in April, according to the water resources ministry in mid-July, marking the start of a month-long peak flood control window. More than 600 rivers have since risen above warning levels – a 35% jump from the average for the same period over the past five years.
In the south-western city of Chongqing, a huge landslide after torrential rain killed at least 11 people and left 50 missing, with rescue efforts still ongoing. Separately, a flash flood at a scenic camping spot in the north-central province of Gansu left 10 people dead and injured 23 others.
The flood season across the region has been exacerbated by successive storms. Typhoon Noul, the strongest to make landfall in China so far this year, prompted the evacuation of more than 890,000 people in Guangdong as of Sunday evening, according to provincial authorities. In early July, Typhoon Maysak inundated parts of Guangxi and swept through commercial snake farms, allowing hundreds of snakes to escape.
Forecasters have warned that more wet weather is on the way. Much of northern China, including Beijing, is expected to receive 20% to 50% more rain than usual, while four to six typhoons are forecast to make landfall in or affect the country this summer, above the average of 4.2, according to the China Meteorological Administration.
Taiwan, an island that lies in the path of typhoons in the north-west Pacific, has also seen a rise in extreme rainfall. In June, repeated downpours caused more than NT$330m (about US$10.2m) in agricultural losses across Taiwan, according to the agriculture ministry, while the capital Taipei recorded its highest monthly rainfall in more than a century.
The extreme weather across the region can clearly be linked to climate change. Climate scientists have long predicted that large areas of Asia will disproportionately suffer from more intense heat, humidity and drought as a result of climate disruption caused by the burning of gas, oil and coal. The most recent report by the United Nations’ Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change said rising temperatures raise the threat of “floods in monsoon regions in south, south-east and east Asia, and glacier melting in the Hindu Kush Himalaya region”.
And World Weather Attribution scientists have warned that extreme rainfall from cyclones is being “supercharged” in south-east Asia, with a clear pattern of increasingly heavy rain over recent decades.
The year 2025 saw devastating storms and rainfall across the region. It also saw ocean temperatures rise to record heights. So far, this year has brought record-breaking heatwaves. Extreme rainfall is more common and more intense because of human-caused climate breakdown across most of the world, particularly in Europe, most of Asia, central and eastern North America, and parts of South America, Africa and Australia. This is because warmer air can hold more water vapour and flooding has most likely become more frequent and severe in these locations as a result.
“More intense rainfall is an expected consequence of us heating the planet by burning fossil fuels and building up more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. A warmer atmosphere can carry more water, so when it rains, it rains harder. Also hotter conditions cause air to rise faster and drive more intense thunderstorms,” said Richard Betts, head of the climate impacts strategic area at the Met Office Hadley Centre.
The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) in providing aid helped the Guardian obtain interviews with those affected.
Dr Hosam Faysal, the head of IFRC’s country delegation in Afghanistan, said “these are the very real, humanitarian effects of a changing climate … becoming increasingly volatile”.
Faysal urged governments to ensure there was more investment in locally-led preparedness and mitigation in order to reduce the loss of life and suffering before climate-related disasters happened.
“The coming forecast El Niño is a clear example – waiting to respond to the extreme needs we can see coming only once they arrive will cost lives.”
- 
  Research by Yu-chen Li

title: AusAlert test will blast emergency warning siren over most phones in Australia on Monday. Hereâs what to know
text:
The AusAlert national emergency warning test message and sound will be sent to mobile phones and some smart watches and tablets across Australia at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
The AusAlert national emergency warning test message and sound will be sent to mobile phones and some smart watches and tablets across Australia at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July. Photograph: Mick Tsikas/AAP
AusAlert test will blast emergency warning siren over most phones in Australia on Monday. Here’s what to know
This article is more than 1 month old
National emergency test alert will be sent to all compatible mobile devices on 27 July, with domestic violence advocates advising how to turn off safe phones
Virtually every phone in the country will blare an emergency siren at 2pm AEST on Monday 27 July as part of the first Australia-wide test of a new national warning system called AusAlert.
Most phones, and some smartwatches and tablets, will receive a pop-up notification and an alert sound that cannot be silenced – even if your device is on “do not disturb” or silent mode.
AusAlert is Australia’s new national warning system, which will send emergency messages to mobile devices during local and widespread disasters.
Authorities currently use SMS texts to alert people about safety information. The new system will instead send a mass broadcast via mobile phone towers, with an alert popping up on devices, similar to a phone notification.
It will launch nationally in October, months after the national alert test.
What will happen during the national test?
“On Monday 27 July 2026, a test alert will be sent to all mobile devices in Australia. This includes most phones, and some smart watches and tablets,” the National Emergency Management Agency (Nema) advises.
Users will hear a siren and see a pop-up notification on their phone, which will look different depending on the device, but with text including “TEST MESSAGE” and “NO ACTION IS REQUIRED”.
Video of the AusAlert test
“What people should expect to hear is a siren that will last for about 10 seconds,” said Pat Hetherington, the interim coordinator general at Nema.
He said it would be “loud enough to get people’s attention” but quieter than a fire alarm.
“It will be noticeable, but it won’t won’t be too over the top.”
What time is the AusAlert test around Australia?
There have been local tests, but Monday will be the first nationwide test, occurring at 2pm AEST, which is:
2pm for New South Wales, Victoria, the ACT, Queensland and Tasmania.
1.30pm in the Northern Territory and South Australia.
12pm in Western Australia.
Why is the AusAlert emergency warning system test needed?
Hetherington said AusAlert came from a recommendation of the royal commission into the 2019-20 black summer bushfires, which called for a nationally consistent warning system.
“The existing system is based on standard SMS capability, and throughout a series of emergencies and disasters, that system has had real latency in terms of people receiving the messages,” he said.
“You [could] get network congestion, text messages may not come through in a timely way … or come through at all, dependent upon who your provider is.”
Kristy McBain, the federal emergency management minister whose electorate of Eden-Monaro was hit by the black summer bushfires, said some people in her area didn’t receive emergency text alerts during that disaster because their phone provider was unavailable.
The new system allows nationwide alerts as well as localised “geofenced” alerts such as for floods or even warnings to boil water in emergency situations.
The emergency services minister, Kristy McBain, says the AusAlert is ‘far superior’ to current warning systems. Photograph: James Ross/AAP
McBain said AusAlert was a “far superior” system and would reach “more people in a more timely manner” than current warning systems used by state governments. Existing systems will still be used in future, with McBain describing AusAlert as “another tool in the toolkit”.
Will every phone ring or make a sound during the alert test at 2pm AEST?
Essentially, yes. Hetherington said phones made after 2019 should receive the alert, but some older phones may not.
The alert will come through on all compatible devices even if you are on a call, or if the phone is on silent. Nema has advice that about 80% of Apple iPhones will ring, and some 16m Android devices.
“The only way to not receive a critical alert is to turn your mobile device off or switch it to ‘airplane mode’,” Nema advised.
The agency said the alert will go to:
iPhone models 11 and up running iOS 26.4 or later.
Apple Watch models SE2, SE3, Series 6 and up running watchOS 26.4 or later.
Android devices running Android 12 or later.
Older Androids, or those not using iOS or Android “might still receive AusAlerts”, Nema said, but Apple iPads will not.
Hetherington and Nema’s deputy coordinator general, Katarina Carroll, said the agency had engaged with “thousands” of groups including schools, businesses and even funeral associations to warn of the alert test.
They said it was important to run the test during an “ordinary” time of day so people knew what to expect in future.
But noting some people may find it inconvenient to have a loud siren ring alert, such as during an important meeting or a funeral, Hetherington and Carroll said “if you have your phone off an hour before and an hour after [2pm AEST], we’re confident you won’t receive that message”.
Other countries around the world have had problems in testing or using such systems, with alerts delayed or not arriving at all. Nema said it had “learned a lot” from tests around the world and it was well prepared for Monday.
What about ‘safe phones’ for those experiencing domestic and family violence?
Domestic and family violence advocates have raised concerns about the risk of the alert exposing “safe phones”, or devices kept hidden for safety reasons by those experiencing violence.
Nema said the agency had engaged with family violence experts about the test, including assisting advocates to disseminate safety information, and posting a safety guide on its website.
Hetherington said phones switched off or on airplane mode would not receive the alert, and said: “The message for safe phones and hidden phones is very much [to switch off for] a 24-hour period.”
Carroll added: “The advice is if there’s anything that’s happening [during the test], have it off for an hour or so. But certainly for domestic and family violence, there’s that broader advice for that extension of time [24 hours].”
Groups such as the Women’s Safety Commissioner, DV Connect and the Council of Single Mothers and their Children have issued safety advisories to this effect.
What do I have to do when I receive the AusAlert?
Nothing at all. The test requires no action.
However, Hetherington encouraged Australians to answer a survey or give feedback after the test to help Nema assess the success of the trial and any changes that may be needed.
“People should read the message. But it is a test that doesn’t require people to do anything,” he said.
“We’re obviously interested in hearing if people haven’t received the message.”
When will AusAlert be used for real?
Nema suggests the warnings could be used for legitimate hazards such as bushfires, floods, cyclones and earthquakes; serious public safety issues or terrorism; biosecurity incidents; and major public health incidents.
States and territories will be able to send alerts.
“I would expect some states to use it quite a lot, particularly where you want information to get out almost in real time,” Hetherington said.

title: At least two people missing in West Virginia after torrential rain causes flash floods
text:
Patrick Morrisey, the West Virginia governor, said at least two people were unaccounted for in Upshur county, after torrential rain caused flash floods in parts of the state.
Speaking at a news conference, Morrisey said that during search-and-recovery operations state police found an overturned vehicle in Upshur county believed to be “connected to two individuals who were reported missing”.
“Because of dangerous conditions and a significant amount of debris surrounding the vehicle, responders have still be unable to safely access it,” he said, adding that the efforts were continuing.
Morrisey said: “Once responders are able to safely complete the operation, and there’s been formal identification, as well as notification of next of kin, we will release additional information. Our thoughts are obviously with the families who are going through a very, very difficult time.”
On Wednesday, Morrisey said West Virginia remained in a “phase of search and rescue” with teams working to “identify any individual who we might be able to save”.
“We are concerned about loss of life,” Morrisey said.
Earlier in the week Morrisey declared a state of emergency for all 55 counties across West Virginia and issued a “state of preparedness” as severe weather approached, directing state agencies to stand ready to respond.
Initially, about 100 national guard members were deployed to the hardest-hit areas. Another 400 national guard members were then mobilized to support flood-response operations.
The governor’s office said on Tuesday “a series of storm systems” had “moved across the state” and produced “severe thunderstorms, damaging winds, torrential rainfall, mudslides and rapidly rising water in many communities”. The most significant impacts, the office said, were reported in Lewis, Pleasants and Upshur counties, where flooding and related damage had prompted emergency response efforts.
Morrisey on Thursday said “a lot of homes” were “destroyed” and businesses “harmed”, and said the state would ensure that “those damage assessments get reported”. He urged people to fill out an online form to report damage.
Images and videos shared online show vehicles submerged in parking lots, flooded homes and neighborhood streets transformed into waterways.
On Wednesday, Morrisey described the storms as “quite extraordinary” and said “we had a significant amount of rainfall occur within a very short period of time”.
In Upshur county, he said, about 4.5in (11cm) of rain fell in just 37 minutes. “When things like that happen, there’s no place for the water to go,” he said. “And so that’s one of the reasons why you see here in Upshur county that there’s still a fair amount of water covering parts of the city.”
The governor also said his office was aware that “there are still many people who are without power here in the mountain state” and said that “utility crews are working very very hard to get to all these places”.
As of Thursday morning, there were more than 6,000 residents in West Virginia without power, according to Poweroutage.us.
Morrisey said “[what] we’re hearing is that the main line of the severe weather has moved through” and warned: “The ground is still saturated and the rivers remain high, so we’re going to continue to consult with the National Weather Service and monitor all the conditions around the clock.”
He said: “This is a time for West Virginians to come together to do everything possible, not only to pray for all those who are affected, but we’re going to need a lot of help in the days and weeks ahead. Let’s help these communities rebuild.”
The West Virginia department of transportation said crews were out in “full force” working to “clear debris, remove downed trees and safely reopen roads”.
The National Weather Service in Charleston, West Virginia, said “quiet weather is expected through the end of the work week, with patchy dense fog possible each night”, but that “chances of showers and thunderstorms begin working back into the area over the weekend”.

title: Tropical storm Bertha makes landfall in Louisiana with 45mph winds
text:
Tropical storm Bertha made landfall in St Bernard parish, on the Gulf coast south-east of New Orleans, Louisiana, on Wednesday afternoon, the US national hurricane center said.
The Miami-based forecaster added that maximum sustained winds were estimated to be 45mph (75km/h) with higher gusts.
The weakening storm had been creeping along the coast, but still spinning off strong winds far from its center and closing beaches from Florida to Mississippi. Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season that is now unfolding.
Elsewhere, a band of extreme weather that ripped through states including Kentucky and West Virginia on Tuesday night sparked devastating tornadoes and record flash flooding that left dozens of people trapped in their houses and vehicles, and injured several others.
First responders in one West Virginia county were overwhelmed by the volume of calls as waters rose to unprecedented levels, with rescuers cutting through attic roofs to free those inside. Patrick Morrisey, the governor, placed all 55 counties under a state of emergency. He sent 100 national guard members to the hardest-hit areas in the northern part of the state, and an additional 200 national guard members were due to arrive on Wednesday.
“State and local agencies will remain on the ground for as long as it takes to help affected communities,” Morrisey said in a statement.
In Kentucky, there were reports of multiple tornadoes, flooding, landslides and widespread damage to infrastructure, including a bridge that was swept away.
The threat from extreme weather conditions continued through the mid-Atlantic region on Wednesday, AccuWeather said, after damaging winds also stretched into New Jersey, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania.
“By Wednesday, the severe weather threat will shift southward, focusing on southern Delaware and southeastern Maryland into central and southeastern Virginia, and central and eastern North Carolina,” the weather outlet warned in a bulletin.
Officials in Buckhannon, West Virginia, were assessing damage early on Wednesday after flooding they described as “catastrophic”. MetroNews, citing data from the National Weather Service (NWS), said the Sand Run stream crested at 10.63ft (3.24 meters) on Tuesday night, surpassing the 8.3ft mark set during floods in 1985.
Local media in Upshur county reported “chaotic radio traffic” between first responders and scenes including: “People hanging from trees. Bridges destroyed. Roads washed out. Structures floating down creeks. Entire families in the water. Cars abandoned. Houses colliding into one another.”
Robbie Skinner, the Buckhannon mayor, told MetroNews on Tuesday night: “I’ve never seen anything like this, and I’ve lived here for 37 years. The river is still rising, we’re not done yet.”
Outlets reported that water rescue crews in swift boats were moving from property to property cutting holes in roofs to free people trapped in their attics, and dozens of people being evacuated by boat from a flooded hotel.
Tens of thousands of customers were still without electricity in Ohio, Virginia and West Virginia on Wednesday morning, poweroutage.us said, with many more having been restored.
Some of the worst damage from tornadoes came in Kentucky. Multiple people were injured in Grayson county, officials there said, one with serious injuries requiring hospital admission. Up to 25 buildings were severely damaged or “completely gone”, Carey Sims, the county’s director of emergency management, told WDRB News.
The NWS office in Louisville said in a post on X that it planned to conduct damage surveys in at least four areas and across seven counties of the state on Wednesday morning.
The Associated Press and Reuters contributed reporting

title: Millions face long-term coastal flooding risk in UK without climate action, scientists warn
text:
Up to 13 million people in the UK face the long-term risk of coastal flooding due to the climate crisis, scientists have warned, with a “reasonable worst-case scenario” suggesting the need for the large-scale movement of populations away from a dramatically reshaped coast.
Even if today’s global pledges to cut carbon pollution are met, about 1.4 million more people will be exposed to coastal floods in 2200 and 1.7 million in 2300 due to the sea level rise driven by melting ice caps and warming oceans.
While this is far in the future, action today to cut emissions and plan future settlements and flood defences could prevent such leaps in flood risk becoming inevitable, the experts said. Keeping within the Paris agreement targets would cut the number of people exposed in 2300 by 1 million, they said.
Sea level has risen by about 20cm around the UK in the last century and is accelerating. A further 40cm to 60cm by 2100 is already baked in, meaning about half a million more people will be at risk of their homes being flooded, on top of the 2.5 million already in danger near the coasts. Lincolnshire and the Humber estuary are most in danger.
However, scientists are concerned that the gradual rise in sea levels seen so far could change rapidly if ice sheets start a runaway collapse into the oceans, instead of just melting slowly in place. In this scenario, the UK could suffer 15 metres of sea level rise by 2300, swamping large parts of London and many other places, the researchers found.
“[Planners] who only consider changes over the coming century may have a false impression of the true risk landscape given the potential for post-2100 acceleration of sea level rise,” the researchers concluded in their study published in the journal Nature Communications. “It is inevitable that a combination of additional or enhanced flood defences and managed retreat will be necessary to mitigate against post-2100 flood risk.”
Prof Matt Palmer at the University of Bristol, who led the research, said: “The oceans and ice-covered parts of the world respond very slowly to global warming, which makes sea level rise the ‘sleeping giant’ of climate change. The result is that sea-level rise is locked-in for centuries to come.”
Dr Rob Larter, at the British Antarctic Survey and not involved in the study, said it was a sobering analysis: “It shows how the UK is likely to have to adapt to several metres of sea level rise over coming centuries. The higher impact [scenarios] presented in this study need to be considered as genuine possibilities rather than unlikely scare stories.”
The research is the first to quantify the number of UK people at threat from coastal flooding under long-term sea level rise. It combined sea level rise projections for the UK with a detailed flood model developed by the Bristol company Fathom. Sea level rise is greater in England and Wales than in Scotland and Northern Ireland as the latter countries were pushed down during the last ice age and are still slowly rebounding.
The study did not factor in greater surges from storms supercharged by global heating or future changes in population. It also did not consider future changes to flood defences, which are highly uncertain, but instead set out the level of likely threat in different scenarios.
Dr Joanne Williams, at the National Oceanography Centre in Southampton, said: “It is useful to consider [worst-case scenarios], because it shows how expensive and challenging it will be if we do not act on climate, with very large areas at new risk. Upgrading existing flood defence lines to the levels required by these high-end scenarios would be extremely challenging.”
Coastal flooding is just one type of flood risk in the UK. River and flash flooding already affect more people and are worsening as the warming climate leads to more intense rainfall.

title: Rescuers in Afghanistan search for missing and dead after flash floods destroy homes
text:
Rescue crews in Afghanistan are searching for survivors and bodies among the rubble of houses destroyed by devastating flash floods that authorities said had killed nearly two dozen people and left more than 100 people missing.
The Afghanistan national disaster management authority said on Tuesday that 23 people had died, 80 had been injured and more than 100 were missing after floods struck the eastern province of Nuristan on Monday, causing an undetermined number of buildings to collapse. The provincial capital city of Parun was among the areas affected, authorities said.
More extreme weather has been forecast, with heavy rain, thunderstorms, strong winds accompanied by dust and sand, and flash floods predicted in 10 of the country’s 34 provinces, the ministry of transport and civil aviation’s meteorology department said on Monday evening. The ministry warned people to avoid riverbanks and other areas at risk of flooding.
Afghanistan is highly vulnerable to extreme weather events, with snow and heavy rain that trigger flash floods, often killing dozens or even hundreds of people at a time. In 2024, more than 300 people died in springtime flash floods. Earlier this year, at least 110 people were killed by widespread flooding and landslides in several parts of the country.
Decades of conflict, along with poor infrastructure, a struggling economy, deforestation and the intensifying effects of climate breakdown have amplified the impact of such disasters, particularly in remote areas where many homes are built of mud and offer limited protection against sudden deluges or heavy snowfall.

title: Tropical Storm Bertha heads for land as Hurricane Fausto forms in eastern Pacific
text:
Tropical Storm Bertha formed on Monday evening in the Gulf of Mexico south of the Florida Panhandle as it drifts erratically toward populated coastal areas, bringing a threat of heavy rain, storm surge and damaging wind gusts.
Meanwhile, in the eastern Pacific Ocean, Hurricane Fausto formed far from Mexico’s Baja California peninsula and posed no threat to land on Monday night.
The center of Bertha was located about 110 miles (180km) south of Panama City, Florida. Maximum sustained winds were about 40mph (64km/h), according to an evening advisory from the Miami-based National Hurricane Center.
The slow-moving storm has been drifting erratically, but is expected to stay near or along the northern Gulf coast early this week, bringing heavy rainfall to areas of northern Florida, Alabama, Mississippi and Louisiana as it pushes westward toward Texas. Forecasters said some additional strengthening is expected in the coming hours.
Bertha is the second tropical storm of the Atlantic hurricane season and is expected to make landfall in south-east Louisiana on Wednesday. Tropical Storm Arthur last month brought heavy rainfall to the south-eastern United States.
A storm surge watch was in effect from the Alabama-Florida border westward to the mouth of the Mississippi River in Louisiana. A tropical storm watch, meanwhile, extended from the Mississippi-Alabama border to the line separating Louisiana’s Jefferson and Plaquemines parishes, the NHC added.
The NHC said the storm surge watch indicated a risk of life-threatening coastal flooding from rising water moving inland from the shoreline within the next 48 hours. Combined with high tide, storm surge could flood normally dry coastal areas along parts of the northern Gulf coast.
Water levels could rise by 2-4ft (60-120cm) from the mouth of the Mississippi River to the Alabama-Florida border, with 1-3ft of surge possible across portions of coastal Louisiana and Florida, including Lake Pontchartrain.
The depression was also expected to produce widespread rainfall totals of 2-4in, with isolated amounts of up to 8in through Friday from western Florida to the middle Texas coast. The heavy rain could trigger flash flooding in some areas, while an isolated tornado or two was possible across Florida’s Big Bend region.
Fausto gained hurricane status on Monday night and was about 745 miles south-west of the southern tip of the Baja California peninsula, forecasters said.
The NHC said Fausto had top sustained winds of 75mph and was moving to the west-northwest at 9mph.
No coastal watches or warnings were in effect though ocean swells generated by the storm could pummel the Baja California coast and cause life-threatening surf and rip tide conditions, the center said.

title: Weather tracker: Flooding and landslides hit large parts of Asia
text:
Large parts of Asia were hit by devastating flooding and landslides last week, leading to multiple deaths, as torrential rain battered Vietnam, southern China and South Korea.
According to the National Centre for Hydro-Meteorological forecasting in Vietnam, the Phuc Than weather station recorded 206mm of rain in 24 hours, from last Thursday into Friday, which caused homes to be swept away, power cuts and destroyed 238 hectares (588 acres) of farmland. Flash flooding swept through the village of Muong Than in southern Vietnam early on Friday morning, causing the deaths of at least four people and leaving four others missing. South Korea also had rainfall totals reaching almost 200mm with a station in Paju, just to the north of Seoul, recording 192.5mm, causing homes and roads to become flooded.
Meanwhile, many countries in Europe continue to suffer under a prolonged heatwave as a southerly flow brings hot air from Africa. A red weather warning was issued for southern Italy on Saturday, which remains in place. Temperatures are expected to exceed 40C in Palermo, a city in Sicily, on Monday and Tuesday, which is more than 10C above the average. This plume of heat is then expected to migrate westwards through this week into Spain, causing temperatures to soar above 40C across large parts of Spain, potentially even exceeding 45C.
Over in the eastern Pacific Ocean, Tropical Storm Elida developed last week, with peak recorded wind speeds of 70mph, just short of the 74mph required to reach a category 1 hurricane. Storm Elida will move northwards through this week and weaken without passing over any land. Another tropical storm developed in the eastern Pacific on Sunday and was named Fausto; it’s expected to move westwards and develop into a category 2 hurricane later this week.
Meanwhile, the western Atlantic has had a quiet tropical hurricane season with no hurricanes and only one tropical storm named Storm Arthur. However, at the time of writing, there is a tropical depression in the Gulf of Mexico which is expected to develop into a tropical storm and move along the south coast of Louisiana and Texas. Once this system develops into a tropical storm, it should be named Bertha. It is not expected to develop strong enough winds to develop into a hurricane, but it still poses a flooding risk to the south-east of the US.

title: Country diary: Beaver-style flood defences take root amid a hosepipe ban
text:
Catkins fall from the sweet chestnut trees like long yellow streamers from a party. More than 20 wasps fret over the bonnet of my car, feeding off something – maybe sticky tree sap or dead insects.
The hay crop is in. No high yields, but better than last year. Two red kites hunt over the coumarin-sweet cut meadows and the swallows glide low. The empty fields usually beckon a gallop, but the ground rings out under hoof like a metalled road. If there is no rain, a second crop seems unlikely.
A hosepipe ban has just been announced, with East Anglia the driest region in the country. Imagining a deluge seems almost impossible, yet my village, a few miles away, has been planning for just that.
In December 2020, the rain didn’t stop. Drains couldn’t cope with the rush of water off the fields. The street became a fast, shallow, brown river and sandbags weren’t enough to stop homes from flooding. The road is often submerged, enough to stop smaller cars. The flood signs go up, and volunteers venture out to keep the drains clear. That Christmas was the worst.
But something has changed. When I walk down the aptly named Wash Lane, where a deep crevice holds the now completely dry watercourse, there are four large constructions. Made from wood, they are “leaky dams” or logjams, designed to collect debris and naturally slow the flow of water.
This has cost Norfolk county council more than £35,000. The work is inspired by the original and best ecosystem engineers: beavers. They fell trees for constructing their dams and lodges, and in doing so reduce water flow and create pools for dragonflies and amphibians to breed.
We are beaver-less round here. There are a handful of released beavers in Norfolk, some of which have bred successfully, but not close by.
Yet while these timber barriers have been built to slow water naturally, the surrounding fields are proposed for a large-scale solar development, which could alter rainwater runoff. Climate change brings us extremes of weather, but surely the solutions must be beaver-clever, working for the health of the whole landscape and leaving more room for nature, not less.

title: Five family members found dead after flash flood in Utah canyon, police say
text:
Five family members who had set out for a day of hiking were killed after a flash flood swept through canyons of southern Utah on Friday, law enforcement officials said.
The victims were a captain in the Provo fire department, his wife and their sons, according to fire officials. A daughter who was not on the trip survived.
The family arrived on Friday at Sunglow campground in a scenic red rock canyon near Bicknell, Utah, for their day excursion, the Wayne county sheriff’s office said.
“It is believed the family fell victim to flooding caused by heavy rains,” the sheriff’s office said in a news release.
Although the sheriff’s office did not identify the victims, the Provo fire department confirmed in a social media post that a fire captain, Spencer Long, and his family members were killed.
“We are absolutely heartbroken by the death of Captain Spencer Long and his family. Our thoughts are with his family, friends, and colleagues during this difficult time,” officials with the fire department wrote.
On Friday night, deputies were called to the campground after the body of a young man was found in the flood wash. The bodies of the other family members were recovered later on Friday and Saturday.
Meanwhile, tributes poured in for the family.
Long; his wife, Katrina; and their sons Reid, Thayne and Gage died in the devastating floods, according to a GoFundMe site set up by a family friend to support the Longs’ daughter as she navigates the loss of her family.
“Spencer and Katrina were loving, devoted parents whose greatest joy was their family. They touched the lives of so many with their kindness, generosity, and unwavering love,” Bree Nielson wrote on the page.
Katrina Long was the co-founder of a medical spa. “Our hearts are with all of their loved ones as we grieve the unimaginable loss of Katrina, her husband, and their three beautiful boys,” Summit Medical Spa posted on Facebook.

title: Flash flood warnings strike north-east US amid wildfire smoke from Canada
text:
Saturday is delivering a double dose of dangerous weather across the north-eastern US, with smoky skies from Canadian wildfires giving way to severe thunderstorms that have already triggered a flash flood warning as torrential rain pounds parts of the region.
After a brief break on Friday, smoke from the wildfires moved back into New York City and surrounding communities on Saturday, sending air quality back into unhealthy levels.
Conditions are expected to gradually improve as shifting winds push the smoke away, but those same changing conditions are fueling a new threat: strong to severe thunderstorms that are expected to sweep across much of the region, clearing the haze while bringing the potential for dangerous weather.
The first wave of powerful storms moved through northern New Jersey and New York City on Saturday, prompting a flash flood warning through 2pm. Videos shared on social media showed water pouring into parts of the city’s vulnerable infrastructure, including Penn Station.
By the afternoon, more than 2.5in (6cm) of rain had fallen in some locations, with flooding either under way or expected in areas covered by the warning. Neighborhoods including Jamaica, Crown Heights, Forest Hills, Ozone Park, Brooklyn Heights, Park Slope, Woodside and Greenpoint were among those affected.
Forecasters warn the storms could produce torrential rainfall capable of causing flash flooding, damaging wind gusts and even isolated tornadoes before the day is over. Hail is also possible. The National Weather Service has placed much of the tri-state area under a level 3 (out of 5) risk. Unlike the more typical scattered severe storms, this level indicates numerous severe storms are likely.
Meanwhile, Texas continues to battle the aftermath of days of destructive storms and historic rainfall. Although the prolonged rain has ended across Texas Hill Country, forecasters are now closely monitoring major rivers expected to surge south through the weekend.
The Devils River in south-west Texas was forecast to reach major flood stage on Saturday morning and could climb as high as 22ft (6.7 meters), according to the National Weather Service; the flood stage for the Devils River is 5ft (1.5 meters) in that area, the NWS said.
The Rio Grande is expected to peak at 21ft (6.4 meters) by Sunday morning; minor flooding in the Laredo area is at 8ft (2.4 meters).
Emergency crews carried out more rescues on Friday as additional heavy rain expanded the flood threat. The flooding has killed at least two people and left hundreds more needing rescue.
More than 2ft (60cm) of rain fell in some areas during a week of relentless downpours. While rainfall was expected to ease, another round of showers pushed already swollen rivers even higher and flooded rural communities near the Mexico border that had largely escaped the worst of the earlier damage.
Near Ozona, roughly 200 miles (320km) west of San Antonio, flood waters overtopped Interstate 10. More than 50 people were rescued by boat from flooded apartment complexes, and an RV park was overwhelmed by rising water. In Uvalde county, part of a bridge collapsed over the Nueces River after the region received months’ worth of rainfall in just a matter of days.
In Cincinnati, Ohio, residents of the Hyde Park neighborhood said it took just 20 to 30 minutes for heavy rain to escalate into a dangerous flooding situation, reported WCPO.
Across several states, communities are continuing cleanup efforts and assessing the damage left behind by powerful flooding. Long sections of highway were submerged, forcing numerous drivers to pull over as flood waters covered the roadways.

title: Climate change driving more rains that lead to deadly flash floods, experts say
text:
Climate change is driving increasingly common bouts of heavy rain in the US that cause deadly and damaging flash floods that will only become more frequent and intense as the crisis worsens, experts say.
A year after deadly flooding in central Texas that swept through a children’s summer camp, the state and other parts of the United States are again experiencing unusually heavy rain. Over the last month, states like Alaska, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, Ohio and Pennsylvania have all experienced record rainfall, causing flash flooding across the country.
Despite climate scientists’ forecasts and tragic events like the flood at Camp Mystic in Texas, experts argue that some government officials are not investing enough money and political capital to upgrade infrastructure and restrict where people can build to accommodate the new, wetter normal.
“We have basically built for a climate that no longer exists, and retrofitting our infrastructure is a slow and expensive process,” said Alice Hill, a senior fellow for energy and the environment at the Council on Foreign Relations. “Adding to that challenge is the fact that in many places, climate change – the term – is a dirty word, and that can reduce the initiative to make sure that any investments made today can carry the excess rainfall.”
Heavy precipitation events have become more common because the oceans and air have warmed, which has caused evaporation to increase and put more water vapor into the atmosphere, said Jennifer Francis, senior scientist with the Woodwell Climate Research Center.
That vapor is a greenhouse gas, which creates a positive feedback loop. It’s also “a fuel for storms” because hurricanes feed off it, and it provides storms “more water to work with”, Francis explained.
That heavy rainfall is more likely to cause flash flooding in hilly areas where the soil does not allow much water to enter the ground; densely populated places where highways and buildings reduce the amount of water absorbed by the Earth; and canyons, where hikers can be trapped by rapidly rising water, according to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
Much of the country is not prepared for the extreme weather, experts say. That is in part because some cities still use pipes that are more than a century old.
“That system just can’t carry this kind of rainfall,” Hill said.
Cities like Houston and New York City have also continued to let developers build in floodplains.
In central Texas, for example, much of the landscape is hilly, which leaves limited space for construction, said Jim Blackburn, an environmental law professor at Rice University in Houston.
“So that flat land next to the [Guadalupe River] has always been, from a Texas viewpoint, prime for development,” Blackburn said.
To protect against catastrophic property damage and deaths, governments must introduce regulations to prohibit building homes and businesses in flood plains, Blackburn said.
But in Texas – among other states – people “generally resist flooding regulations and try to find our way around them as best they can”, Blackburn said.
At Camp Mystic, where 25 campers, two counselors and the director died during the flooding, the owners had successfully appealed to the Federal Emergency Management Agency (Fema) to have some of its buildings removed from a 100-year flood map, which allowed the camp to operate and expand in the potentially dangerous area.
In Harris county, Texas, where Hurricane Harvey in 2017 caused more than $125bn in damage, homeowners and developers have appealed to Fema to have more than 6,500 homes removed from the floodplain map, which allows them to avoid stricter building rules and flood insurance costs, the Houston Chronicle reported.
Now Fema is drafting a new flood zone map to adjust for the increased rainfall rate.
“People use these maps for decisions on buying real estate. They use these maps to determine the vulnerability of hazardous waste facilities, various types of sensitive private-sector and government facilities, and hospitals. We want those to be free from flooding during flood emergencies because, among other things, we need to get to emergency rooms,” Blackburn said.
Real estate developers are concerned about the potential new map because it could create liability issues and make properties in the new floodplain less attractive to buyers, Blackburn said.
“They may have promoted it as not being in the floodplain, and they will have to go out and change all those statements,” Blackburn said.
People in Texas and other red states who advocate for bolstering regulations and infrastructure upgrades to prepare for the increased rainfall must contend with another challenge: distaste for the phrase “climate change”, Blackburn said.
The Republican party of Texas stated in its 2024 platform that it opposes “environmentalism, or ‘climate change’ initiatives, that obstruct legitimate business interests and private property use”.
Efforts to adapt have also encountered obstacles at the federal level. In April 2025, the Trump administration announced that it was eliminating the Building Resilient Infrastructure and Communities program, which had been slated to provide $882m in grants designed to help cities invest in disaster-preparedness projects, like improving stormwater infrastructure. In December, a judge ordered Fema to restore the funding.
A link to the April 2025 press release that announced the end of the “wasteful, politicized grant program” now directs visitors to the Fema homepage, which promotes that it is providing “$600 Million to Help Communities Reduce Flood Risk”.
US cities have invested in the so-called “sponge city” concept, a design to absorb and hold excess water from rainfall.
“That could be through a park, converting impermeable surfaces to permeable surfaces like grass, creating easier water flows for the rainfall,” Hill said.
Despite the Trump administration’s reversal on infrastructure investments, experts say that changing the country so that it can adapt to the additional rainfall will take years.
In the meantime, government officials are trying to keep people safe amid the summer’s heavy rains.
In Missouri, a summer camp experienced flash flooding this month; more than 200 children and staff were evacuated via helicopter. No one at the camp died, but one woman, Faith Gregory, died after her home was swept away.
In Texas, flash flood emergency orders were issued Thursday in two counties, including the one where Camp Mystic was located. Greg Abbott, the Texas governor, reported that two people have died.
“I am informed that the loss of life is not a camper,” he said, noting that more than 70 people had been rescued. “Our No 1 focus is saving lives.”

title: At least two dead as life-threatening flash floods and storms hit central Texas
text:
At least two people have died as “life-threatening” flooding takes hold in south-central Texas, where up to 28in of rain has already fallen in some areas – just a year after the same region endured catastrophic flooding that killed more than 100 people.
Flash-flood emergencies were issued on Thursday for parts of Kerr and Uvalde counties, where emergency crews performed water rescues, and areas around the Guadalupe River and the Pedernales River, according to morning updates from the National Weather Service (NWS).
Rescuers have been plucking stranded drivers and people trapped in homes since flood waters began rising quickly overnight on Thursday.
“This is a PARTICULARLY DANGEROUS SITUATION. SEEK HIGHER GROUND NOW!” reads an update from the NWS in San Antonio. “Life threatening flash flooding of low water crossings, small creeks and streams, urban areas, highways, streets and underpasses.”
Texas’s governor, Greg Abbott, said in a Thursday press conference that at least two people have died as a result of the flooding: a man who was swept away in an RV near Comfort, and a woman swept away while driving in Uvalde. Abbott said more than 200 people had been rescued, including people trapped in their homes and stranded on flooded roads.
Drones and helicopters are flying over the region still recovering from devastating floods just a year ago, the governor said. In summer camps near the Guadalupe River in Kerr county, the sheriff’s office said all campers were safe.
Flash flood warnings were also in effect for parts of Kinney, Maverick and Zavala counties, among others close to the border with Mexico and in the Texas Hill Country near San Antonio.
A line of storms moving through the region has brought heavy rainfall, causing the Guadalupe River at Comfort, Texas, to rise more than 30ft in a few hours overnight on Thursday. Shelter-in-place orders have been issued for residents in Kerrville and Uvalde, and a broader flood watch remains in effect until Thursday evening.
Officials told the Associated Press that people in Travis county were mostly trapped in trees and on rooftops, while residents in Uvalde were trapped in vehicles overnight.
The catastrophic weather comes just a year after devastating floods during the Fourth of July weekend in the Texas Hill Country killed more than 100 people, including 25 girls and two counselors at Camp Mystic. The Christian girls’ summer camp was located on the banks of the Guadalupe River, where a flash flood emergency was once again in effect on Thursday.
“Our primary focus right now and throughout the remainder of this torrential rain is saving lives,” Abbott said in a Wednesday statement.
Thunderstorms have produced up to 20in of rain in the Uvalde area over the previous 48 hours, while 3-12in of rain have fallen across parts of Bandera, Kerr and Real counties, with officials warning drivers to avoid crossing flooded roads.
“All major highways and many city streets are CLOSED due to flooding and water over the roadway,” the Uvalde county office of emergency management wrote in a post on social media on Thursday. “Please remain at home unless you are in immediate danger or your location is no longer safe.”

title: How global heating supercharged floods in West Africa, displacing thousands
text:
Dozens of people drowned, hundreds had to be rescued and thousands were displaced when floods struck the coasts of west Africa last month.
Now scientists have concluded that the rains that caused the floods were supercharged by climate breakdown. Global heating, they say, turned what should have been a routine weather event into a climate catastrophe.
They also warn that the countries affected must adapt to a frightening new reality. “The climate is changing faster than most nations can adapt,” said Friederike Otto, a professor of climate science at Imperial College London.
“Adapting to these now common events is critical, but so is reducing emissions much further and faster, to allow us time to keep up with the changes we’ve already put into motion. Quite simply, until emissions stop these extremes will only grow worse.”
Residents on the Gulf of Guinea coast expect rain this time of year. Rainy season runs from May until the end of July. Granted, this year it had been particularly heavy, but what began on 20 June caught people by surprise.
Over the course of 72 hours, intense rainfall drenched the densely populated coastal regions of Côte d’Ivoire, Ghana, Togo and Nigeria. More than 140mm of rain fell in some cities in less than a day. The deluge overwhelmed drainage systems, triggering a series of flash floods.
From Lagos to Monrovia in Liberia, the overflow inundated neighbourhoods and washed away markets. It submerged roads and swamped infrastructure. At least 34 people died in Ghana. Five died in Togo. In Côte d’Ivoire, 59 have died as a result of floods since May.
On Thursday, Otto and the World Weather Attribution team said such a deluge was five times more likely in today’s climate. Heavy, three-day downpours in the region had increased in intensity by roughly 23% since record-keeping began, they said.
It will not be long until something similar occurs again, they warned. With the climate 1.4C hotter than before the industrial use of fossil fuels, they expect rainfall of a similar scale to explode above the Gulf of Guinea every two to four years.
To quantify the role the climate crisis had played in the disaster, scientists compared historical weather observations with climate model simulations. They focused specifically on the three most extreme days of rainfall.
Despite climate models often struggling to recreate similar events in regions in the global south, they showed climate change had caused a 4% increase in intensity. The researchers said this made them confident that greenhouse gas emissions had intensified the event.
Joyce Kimutai, who researches extreme weather and climate change at Imperial College London, was the lead author on the study. She said: “Climate models typically struggle to capture the full scale of tropical precipitation trends when we look at extreme events like this one.
“As such, the fact that we found such a role for climate change is significant. Combined with the very wetter trend in the observational-based data, it’s clear that human-caused warming made this event worse, and wetter, with devastating impacts.
“This study is a clear example of the need for international cooperation on climate justice. Industrialised nations have a responsibility to help nations like Togo, Côte d’Ivoire and Ghana to adapt to a worsening problem that they didn’t cause.”

title: South Texas braces for more flooding after US storms strand motorists
text:
Heavy rains in south Texas have washed out highways and stranded motorists, with forecasters warning that more severe weather could bring dangerous flooding to already drenched counties near the border with Mexico.
On Tuesday, storms dumped up to 16in of rain in some rural areas of the state, leading to the dispatch of emergency crews to make at least two dozen rescues across the region. Officials shut down parts of a highway near Uvalde, 80 miles west of San Antonio.
“This is called a typical mid-summer tropical weather pattern that happens in Texas,” Monte Oaks, a meteorologist with the weather service, told the Associated Press.
“About once every five years, we’ll get socked in with a daily recurrence of heavy rain chances that’s generally produced by a stagnant kind of a pattern with a low-pressure center that’s just not moving very fast.”
A flash flood warning is in place in the San Antonio area with torrential downpours expected through the afternoon. Most areas of the metro area are forecast to get between 2 and 4in of rain.
Areas of central Texas also remained at risk of excessive rainfall, including the Hill Country and areas such as Kerrville were at a moderate risk of flash flooding. Two years ago, an area bordering the Guadalupe River experienced flash flooding that killed at least 139 people.
The National Weather Service warned that storms overnight into Wednesday could dump more than a foot of additional rain to some places, creating potentially catastrophic impacts from flash flooding in areas west of San Antonio.
More rain is expected over the next 24 hours, with parts of the region upgraded to a rare level 4 “high” risk of excessive rainfall, indicating that flash flooding is likely. Rainfall totals between 3 and 7in are expected, with isolated higher totals of up to 15in possible.
“Intense rain rates and compounding effects from multiple rounds of storms will result in a dangerous flash flooding threat through Thursday,” the National Weather Service said.
Texas’s governor, Greg Abbott, issued a disaster declaration for 59 Texas counties as severe storms continue to threaten the area.
In a statement on X, Abbott posted a weather map that showed 20in of rain could fall in some areas: “Texans, this is JUST ONE of the weather scenarios I have been referring to in my disaster declaration. Note the amount of rain and the early morning hour it is being predicted. We have deployed rescue teams, Blackhawk helicopters & state personnel to respond to this danger.”
He also advised Texans to “heed weather warnings and local advisories”.

title: Flash flooding in Missouri leaves one person dead as 200 campers are rescued
text:
A woman was found dead in Missouri on Saturday after heavy rainfall battered parts of the state the previous day, forcing numerous emergency rescues and evacuations, including at a summer camp with more than 200 children.
The body of Faith Gregory, who went missing in Missouri’s Crawford county after her home was swept away from its foundation, was found by volunteers late Saturday morning. Her body was discovered about 1.8 miles (3km) downstream from her residence in Huzzah creek, according to the county sheriff’s office.
“This is not the outcome that any of us were hoping for,” sheriff’s office said in a statement. “Our thoughts and prayers are with Faith’s family, friends, and all those affected by this tragic loss.”
There was no longer anyone still unaccounted for in the county, which is about 70 miles (110km) south-west of St Louis.
The National Weather Service (NWS) issued flash flood warnings for the area as thunderstorms piled on one after another.
Several other states also faced the potential for severe thunderstorms and flash flooding as the slow moving storms moved southward.
The NWS said the severe weather affected a wide region stretching from the Ozark Mountains in southern Missouri eastward into much of the Ohio and Tennessee river valleys.
The storms could bring damaging winds, heavy rainfall and scattered flash flooding to the multistate region, with some places seeing impacts into Sunday, the NWS said.
In eastern Tennessee, flooding closed some roads and downed power lines, and authorities from Kentucky to West Virginia told people to be ready to seek higher ground.
Missouri’s emergency management agency warned that while the storms move south and out of the state, further thunderstorms could still bring additional flash flooding, especially in areas that have already received 6 and 12in (15 and 30cm ) of rain.
“It’s very, very popular place for recreation,” Matt Beitscher, a lead meteorologist with the NWS office in St Louis, said of the affected counties. “So there are campgrounds there. There are float trip locations there. A lot of vulnerable populations that would be susceptible to flash flooding.”
Friday’s drenching rains washed away roads around Camp Taum Sauk, trapping children and staff at the site in the small south-eastern community of Lesterville, according Sgt Eddie Young, with the state’s highway patrol. The Army National Guard used Black Hawk helicopters to fly them to a nearby elementary school and reunite them with their families, he said.
The camp thanked emergency crews in a post on Instagram, saying, “We are beyond thankful for your help keeping our camp community safe.”
Meanwhile campers at the Bearcat Getaway campground near the Black River, about 85 miles (140km) south of St Louis, climbed onto a building to get away from the raging waters but it then collapsed, Young said.
“Between the weight and the constant waters underneath it, it just gave away on them,” he said.
Three other people were trapped on trees on the Black River in Reynolds county and were rescued, Young said.
The Missouri governor, Mike Kehoe, declared a state of emergency on Friday and activated a search and rescue team to assist. He said late on Friday that hundreds of people were saved from floodwaters, trees, rooftops and stranded vehicles.
Several major roads were impassable due to flooding and damage, Kehoe said, warning that the Black River continued to rise and was expected to crest at more than 28 feet (8.5 meters) near Annapolis in south-eastern Missouri, which would be a record.
“As recovery efforts continue and additional rain is expected, I urge everyone in flood-prone and low-lying areas to stay weather-aware, have multiple ways of receiving alerts, and be ready to take protective action,” Kehoe said in a statement.
In Reynolds county, two rescue boats capsized in the flooding, but other emergency personnel safely recovered the responders, the sheriff’s office said.
Meanwhile, a widespread and dangerous heatwave was building across the US on Saturday, with triple-digit highs expected in the south-west and Great Plains through the weekend before spreading eastward under a dome of high pressure that meteorologists say could trap oppressive temperatures for a week or more.
Forecasters advised people to stay hydrated and find places to cool off, warning of temperatures 15 to 25F (8 to 14C ) warmer than normal in many areas, including at night – especially bad for people’s health because their bodies won’t have a chance to recover. The heat dome was expected to affect as much as two-thirds of the continental United States.
More than two dozen people died during a previous heatwave that affected much of the US in late June and early July.
Scientists say climate change from burning coal, oil and natural gas is causing intense, long-lasting heatwaves affecting large areas, along with other extreme weather events.
- 
  Guardian staff contributed
